# File: 1.md

RabbitMQ can seem complex at first, but it becomes very approachable once you break it down. Learning it through a **standalone setup**, then with the **pure Java client**, and finally with **Spring Boot** is a great path—it lets you see exactly what Spring Boot is abstracting away for you.

Here is a complete guide to get you started on all three fronts.

---

### 🚀 Part 1: Setting Up a Standalone RabbitMQ Server

For learning and development, the easiest and most standard way to get RabbitMQ running is on an **Ubuntu Linux** system (either a VM, a cloud instance, or WSL on Windows). RabbitMQ requires **Erlang** to run, so the official installation scripts typically handle both dependencies for you.

Here is a widely used method using the official installation script for Ubuntu.

**1. Prepare the Installation Script**
Create a file named `install-rabbitmq.sh` and paste the following script. This script adds the official RabbitMQ repositories and GPG keys, then installs the server.

```bash
#!/bin/sh
sudo apt-get install curl gnupg apt-transport-https -y

## Team RabbitMQ's main signing key
curl -1sLf "https://keys.openpgp.org/vks/v1/by-fingerprint/0A9AF2115F4687BD29803A206B73A36E6026DFCA" | sudo gpg --dearmor | sudo tee /usr/share/keyrings/com.rabbitmq.team.gpg > /dev/null

## Community mirror of Cloudsmith: modern Erlang repository
curl -1sLf https://github.com/rabbitmq/signing-keys/releases/download/3.0/cloudsmith.rabbitmq-erlang.E495BB49CC4BBE5B.key | sudo gpg --dearmor | sudo tee /usr/share/keyrings/rabbitmq.E495BB49CC4BBE5B.gpg > /dev/null

## Community mirror of Cloudsmith: RabbitMQ repository
curl -1sLf https://github.com/rabbitmq/signing-keys/releases/download/3.0/cloudsmith.rabbitmq-server.9F4587F226208342.key | sudo gpg --dearmor | sudo tee /usr/share/keyrings/rabbitmq.9F4587F226208342.gpg > /dev/null

## Add apt repositories maintained by Team RabbitMQ
sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/rabbitmq.list <<EOF
## Provides modern Erlang/OTP releases
deb [arch=amd64 signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/rabbitmq.E495BB49CC4BBE5B.gpg] https://ppa1.rabbitmq.com/rabbitmq/rabbitmq-erlang/deb/ubuntu noble main
deb-src [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/rabbitmq.E495BB49CC4BBE5B.gpg] https://ppa1.rabbitmq.com/rabbitmq/rabbitmq-erlang/deb/ubuntu noble main
## another mirror for redundancy
deb [arch=amd64 signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/rabbitmq.E495BB49CC4BBE5B.gpg] https://ppa2.rabbitmq.com/rabbitmq/rabbitmq-erlang/deb/ubuntu noble main
deb-src [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/rabbitmq.E495BB49CC4BBE5B.gpg] https://ppa2.rabbitmq.com/rabbitmq/rabbitmq-erlang/deb/ubuntu noble main

## Provides RabbitMQ
deb [arch=amd64 signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/rabbitmq.9F4587F226208342.gpg] https://ppa1.rabbitmq.com/rabbitmq/rabbitmq-server/deb/ubuntu noble main
deb-src [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/rabbitmq.9F4587F226208342.gpg] https://ppa1.rabbitmq.com/rabbitmq/rabbitmq-server/deb/ubuntu noble main
## another mirror for redundancy
deb [arch=amd64 signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/rabbitmq.9F4587F226208342.gpg] https://ppa2.rabbitmq.com/rabbitmq/rabbitmq-server/deb/ubuntu noble main
deb-src [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/rabbitmq.9F4587F226208342.gpg] https://ppa2.rabbitmq.com/rabbitmq/rabbitmq-server/deb/ubuntu noble main
EOF

## Update package indices and install RabbitMQ server
sudo apt-get update -y
sudo apt-get install rabbitmq-server -y --fix-missing
```

**2. Run the Script**
Make the script executable and run it with `sudo`.

```bash
chmod +x install-rabbitmq.sh
sudo ./install-rabbitmq.sh
```
The script will install Erlang and the RabbitMQ server as a systemd service, which should start automatically.

**3. Enable the Management Plugin (Highly Recommended)**
The management plugin provides a web-based UI to monitor your queues, exchanges, and connections.

```bash
sudo rabbitmq-plugins enable rabbitmq_management
```
You can then access the UI at `http://localhost:15672/`. The default username and password are both `guest`.

> **Note on the `guest` user**: By default, the `guest` user can only connect from `localhost`. For production or remote access, you must create a new user and grant it permissions.

---

### ☕ Part 2: Using RabbitMQ with "Pure" Java

This approach uses the official `amqp-client` library directly, giving you full control and a clear view of the AMQP protocol operations.

**1. Add the Dependency**
If you are using Maven, add this to your `pom.xml`:

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.rabbitmq</groupId>
    <artifactId>amqp-client</artifactId>
    <version>5.20.0</version> <!-- Use the latest version -->
</dependency>
```

**2. The "Hello World" Example**
The classic first example involves a **Producer** (sender) that sends a message to a queue, and a **Consumer** (receiver) that gets the message from that queue.

**Producer (`Send.java`):**

```java
import com.rabbitmq.client.Channel;
import com.rabbitmq.client.Connection;
import com.rabbitmq.client.ConnectionFactory;

public class Send {
    private final static String QUEUE_NAME = "hello";

    public static void main(String[] argv) throws Exception {
        // 1. Create a connection factory and configure it
        ConnectionFactory factory = new ConnectionFactory();
        factory.setHost("localhost");
        // For a remote server: factory.setUsername("user"); factory.setPassword("pass");

        // 2. Establish a connection and create a channel
        try (Connection connection = factory.newConnection();
             Channel channel = connection.createChannel()) {

            // 3. Declare a queue (idempotent: it will only be created if it doesn't exist)
            channel.queueDeclare(QUEUE_NAME, false, false, false, null);

            // 4. Create and publish the message
            String message = "Hello World!";
            channel.basicPublish("", QUEUE_NAME, null, message.getBytes("UTF-8"));
            System.out.println(" [x] Sent '" + message + "'");
        }
    }
}
```
The `queueDeclare` method is crucial—it ensures the queue exists before you try to send to it.

**Consumer (`Recv.java`):**

```java
import com.rabbitmq.client.Channel;
import com.rabbitmq.client.Connection;
import com.rabbitmq.client.ConnectionFactory;
import com.rabbitmq.client.DeliverCallback;

public class Recv {
    private final static String QUEUE_NAME = "hello";

    public static void main(String[] argv) throws Exception {
        ConnectionFactory factory = new ConnectionFactory();
        factory.setHost("localhost");

        Connection connection = factory.newConnection();
        Channel channel = connection.createChannel();

        channel.queueDeclare(QUEUE_NAME, false, false, false, null);
        System.out.println(" [*] Waiting for messages. To exit press CTRL+C");

        // This callback will be executed whenever a message arrives
        DeliverCallback deliverCallback = (consumerTag, delivery) -> {
            String message = new String(delivery.getBody(), "UTF-8");
            System.out.println(" [x] Received '" + message + "'");
        };

        // Start consuming messages from the queue
        channel.basicConsume(QUEUE_NAME, true, deliverCallback, consumerTag -> {});
    }
}
```
The consumer uses a `DeliverCallback` to process messages asynchronously as they arrive.

---

### 🍃 Part 3: Using RabbitMQ with Spring Boot

Spring Boot's AMQP starter provides a high-level abstraction, making it easier to implement messaging patterns with less boilerplate.

**1. Add Dependencies**
In your `pom.xml`, add the Spring Boot AMQP starter:

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-amqp</artifactId>
</dependency>
```
This transitively includes the `amqp-client` library.

**2. Configure the Connection**
In your `application.yml` or `application.properties`, specify your RabbitMQ connection details:

```yaml
spring:
  rabbitmq:
    host: localhost
    port: 5672
    username: guest
    password: guest
    virtual-host: /
    # Enable publisher confirms for reliability
    publisher-confirm-type: correlated
    # Enable returns if a message cannot be routed
    publisher-returns: true
    # Listener settings for manual acknowledgment (optional but good practice)
    listener:
      simple:
        acknowledge-mode: manual
        prefetch: 10
```
This configuration sets up the connection and enables key reliability features.

**3. Define Exchanges, Queues, and Bindings**
You declare your infrastructure as `@Bean` definitions in a configuration class. Spring will automatically declare these on the broker when the application starts.

```java
import org.springframework.amqp.core.*;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

@Configuration
public class RabbitMQConfig {

    public static final String QUEUE_NAME = "spring-boot-queue";
    public static final String EXCHANGE_NAME = "spring-boot-exchange";
    public static final String ROUTING_KEY = "spring.boot.key";

    @Bean
    public Queue queue() {
        return new Queue(QUEUE_NAME, true); // durable queue
    }

    @Bean
    public TopicExchange exchange() {
        return new TopicExchange(EXCHANGE_NAME);
    }

    @Bean
    public Binding binding(Queue queue, TopicExchange exchange) {
        return BindingBuilder.bind(queue).to(exchange).with(ROUTING_KEY);
    }
}
```
This example defines a durable queue, a topic exchange, and a binding with a specific routing key.

**4. Sending Messages (Producer)**
Spring Boot auto-configures a `RabbitTemplate` bean for sending messages. You can inject and use it directly.

```java
import org.springframework.amqp.rabbit.core.RabbitTemplate;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class MessageProducer {

    private final RabbitTemplate rabbitTemplate;

    public MessageProducer(RabbitTemplate rabbitTemplate) {
        this.rabbitTemplate = rabbitTemplate;
    }

    public void sendMessage(String message) {
        rabbitTemplate.convertAndSend(
            RabbitMQConfig.EXCHANGE_NAME,
            RabbitMQConfig.ROUTING_KEY,
            message
        );
        System.out.println("Sent message: " + message);
    }
}
```
The `convertAndSend` method handles serialization and sending to the correct exchange with the routing key.

**5. Receiving Messages (Consumer)**
Use the `@RabbitListener` annotation to easily create a consumer. Spring will manage the connection and message dispatching.

```java
import org.springframework.amqp.rabbit.annotation.RabbitListener;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class MessageConsumer {

    @RabbitListener(queues = RabbitMQConfig.QUEUE_NAME)
    public void receiveMessage(String message) {
        System.out.println("Received message: " + message);
        // Your business logic here
    }
}
```
The annotated method will be invoked whenever a message is available in the specified queue.

---

### 💎 Key Concepts and Next Steps

To deepen your understanding, focus on these core AMQP concepts:
*   **Exchanges**: The routing agents to which producers send messages. Types include `direct`, `topic`, `fanout`, and `headers`.
*   **Queues**: The buffers that store messages until they are consumed.
*   **Bindings**: The rules that tell an exchange which queues to route messages to, based on routing keys or patterns.
*   **Acknowledgments**: Consumers can manually `ack` or `nack` messages to ensure they are not lost if processing fails.
*   **Dead Letter Queues (DLQ)**: A powerful feature for handling messages that cannot be processed successfully.

A great next step would be to explore the **Spring AMQP Quick Reference** or the official RabbitMQ tutorials for patterns like **Work Queues**, **Publish/Subscribe**, and **Routing**, adapting the pure Java examples to Spring Boot.

I hope this gives you a solid foundation for your RabbitMQ journey. Feel free to ask if you get stuck on any particular part.



<!-- SOURCE: 2.md -->
# File: 2.md

Building on the basics, the next crucial step is moving from "Hello World" to building **reliable, production-ready messaging systems**. This involves understanding how messages are routed, ensuring they are not lost, and handling failures gracefully.

Here is a guide to the advanced concepts and their implementation in Spring Boot and pure Java.

---

### 🔀 1. Mastering Exchange Types: Routing Strategies

Exchanges are the core of RabbitMQ's routing. Choosing the right type is fundamental to your system's architecture.

| Exchange Type | Routing Mechanism | Common Use Case | When to Use |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Direct** | Exact routing key match | Task queues, point-to-point messaging | Simple, explicit routing where each message type has a specific destination. |
| **Fanout** | Broadcast to all bound queues (ignores routing key) | Notifications, cache invalidation, logging | When multiple consumers all need to receive the same message (publish/subscribe). |
| **Topic** | Pattern matching on routing key (e.g., `order.*.eu`) | Event filtering, log routing (e.g., by severity or region) | Complex, hierarchical routing where consumers subscribe to subsets of messages. |
| **Headers** | Matches on message header attributes | Complex routing rules where the routing key is insufficient | Edge cases where routing must be based on multiple attributes rather than a single key string. |

**Implementation Note:** The **Default Exchange** (an empty string `""`) is a direct exchange to which every queue is automatically bound by its name. This is why in the "Hello World" example, you could publish directly to a queue name.

---

### 🛡️ 2. Ensuring Delivery: Publisher Confirms & Returns

A common pitfall is assuming a message was sent successfully just because no exception was thrown. RabbitMQ provides two mechanisms for producers to verify delivery.

*   **Publisher Confirms**: The broker acknowledges that it has **taken responsibility** for the message. This is an asynchronous confirmation from the exchange.
*   **Publisher Returns**: If a message is **routable to an exchange but not to any queue** (e.g., due to a bad routing key), the broker will return it to the producer. This is only triggered if the `mandatory` flag is set on the message.

#### In Spring Boot
You enable these features in your `application.yml`:
```yaml
spring:
  rabbitmq:
    publisher-confirm-type: correlated
    publisher-returns: true
    template:
      mandatory: true # Important: needed for returns to work
```
Then, you configure the callbacks on the `RabbitTemplate` bean:
```java
@Configuration
public class RabbitMQConfig {
    @Autowired
    private RabbitTemplate rabbitTemplate;

    @PostConstruct
    public void configureTemplate() {
        // Confirm callback: Is the message accepted by the exchange?
        rabbitTemplate.setConfirmCallback((correlationData, ack, cause) -> {
            if (!ack) {
                System.err.println("Message not confirmed by broker. Cause: " + cause);
                // Implement retry or alerting logic here
            }
        });

        // Return callback: Was the message routable to a queue?
        rabbitTemplate.setReturnsCallback(returned -> {
            System.err.println("Message returned: " + returned);
            // Handle unroutable messages (e.g., log, send to a parking queue)
        });
    }
}
```

#### In Pure Java
You use the `confirmSelect()` method on the channel and add listeners:
```java
Channel channel = connection.createChannel();
channel.confirmSelect(); // Enable publisher confirms

// Async confirm listener
channel.addConfirmListener((sequenceNumber, multiple) -> {
    System.out.println("Message confirmed: " + sequenceNumber);
}, (sequenceNumber, multiple) -> {
    System.err.println("Message nacked: " + sequenceNumber);
});

// Return listener (for unroutable messages)
channel.addReturnListener(returnedMessage -> {
    System.err.println("Message returned: " + returnedMessage);
});

// Publish with mandatory flag set to true
channel.basicPublish("exchange", "bad.key", true, null, message.getBytes());
```

---

### ⚙️ 3. Consumer Reliability: Manual Acknowledgment & Prefetch

By default, RabbitMQ uses **auto-acknowledgment**, meaning it considers a message delivered as soon as it's sent to a consumer. If the consumer crashes, the message is lost. **Manual acknowledgment** is essential for reliability.

When `acknowledge-mode` is set to `manual`, you must explicitly tell the broker the outcome of processing:

*   **`basicAck(deliveryTag, multiple)`**: Message processed successfully.
*   **`basicNack(deliveryTag, multiple, requeue)`** or **`basicReject`**: Message processing failed.
    *   `requeue = true`: The message is put back in the queue for another attempt.
    *   `requeue = false`: The message is discarded or, more usefully, routed to a Dead Letter Queue (if configured).

**Prefetch (QoS)** works with manual ack to control flow. It limits how many unacknowledged messages a consumer can have at once, preventing it from being overwhelmed.

#### In Spring Boot
Configure in `application.yml`:
```yaml
spring:
  rabbitmq:
    listener:
      simple:
        acknowledge-mode: manual
        prefetch: 10 # Consumer will fetch up to 10 messages at a time
```
In your listener, inject the `Channel` and `deliveryTag` to manually acknowledge:
```java
@RabbitListener(queues = "my.queue")
public void handleMessage(MyMessage message,
                          @Header(AmqpHeaders.DELIVERY_TAG) long deliveryTag,
                          Channel channel) throws IOException {
    try {
        // ... business logic ...
        channel.basicAck(deliveryTag, false); // Success
    } catch (RetryableException e) {
        channel.basicNack(deliveryTag, false, true); // Requeue for retry
    } catch (Exception e) {
        channel.basicNack(deliveryTag, false, false); // Send to DLQ (if configured)
    }
}
```

#### In Pure Java
You must turn off auto-ack when starting the consumer (`autoAck = false`) and manage the ack in your callback:
```java
channel.basicConsume("my.queue", false, (consumerTag, delivery) -> {
    long deliveryTag = delivery.getEnvelope().getDeliveryTag();
    try {
        // ... business logic ...
        channel.basicAck(deliveryTag, false);
    } catch (Exception e) {
        channel.basicNack(deliveryTag, false, true); // Requeue on failure
    }
}, consumerTag -> {});
```

---

### 🪦 4. Handling Failures: Dead Letter Queues (DLQ)

A **Dead Letter Exchange (DLX)** and its bound **DLQ** are where messages are sent when they are "dead-lettered." This happens when:
1.  A message is **rejected** (`basicNack` or `basicReject`) with `requeue=false`.
2.  A message **expires** due to a TTL (Time-To-Live) setting.
3.  The queue length limit is **exceeded**.

#### In Spring Boot
You configure the DLX on the primary queue using `QueueBuilder`:
```java
@Bean
public Queue primaryQueue() {
    return QueueBuilder.durable("primary.queue")
            .deadLetterExchange("dlx.exchange")
            .deadLetterRoutingKey("dlx.key")
            .build();
}

@Bean
public Queue deadLetterQueue() {
    return QueueBuilder.durable("dead.letter.queue").build();
}

@Bean
public DirectExchange deadLetterExchange() {
    return new DirectExchange("dlx.exchange");
}

@Bean
public Binding dlqBinding() {
    return BindingBuilder.bind(deadLetterQueue())
            .to(deadLetterExchange())
            .with("dlx.key");
}
```
A powerful pattern is to have a listener on the DLQ that implements a retry limit before moving the message to a final "parking lot" queue.

#### In Pure Java
You declare the queue arguments when creating the queue:
```java
Map<String, Object> args = new HashMap<>();
args.put("x-dead-letter-exchange", "dlx.exchange");
args.put("x-dead-letter-routing-key", "dlx.key");
channel.queueDeclare("primary.queue", true, false, false, args);
```

---

### 💎 Summary and Next Steps

You now have the tools to build a robust messaging system: **correct routing** (exchanges), **producer reliability** (confirms/returns), **consumer reliability** (manual ack + prefetch), and **failure handling** (DLQ).

A natural next step would be to explore **message persistence** (marking queues as `durable` and messages as `PERSISTENT`) and designing **idempotent consumers** to handle the possibility of duplicate message delivery, which can occur in any at-least-once delivery system.



<!-- SOURCE: 3.md -->
# File: 3.md

Here is the step-by-step continuation, now grounded in a complete **Docker Compose** environment. This setup will host RabbitMQ and serve as the backbone for exploring the advanced reliability patterns in detail.

---

### 🐳 Step 1: The Production-Ready Docker Compose File

A simple RabbitMQ container is fine for a "Hello World," but a reliable setup requires **persistent storage**, **custom credentials** (the default `guest` user is restricted to localhost), and **resource limits**.

Create a file named `docker-compose.yml` in your project root:

```yaml
version: '3.8'

services:
  rabbitmq:
    image: rabbitmq:3.13-management # Includes the Management UI
    container_name: rabbitmq
    hostname: my-rabbit # Fixed hostname for consistent data persistence
    ports:
      - "5672:5672"   # AMQP protocol
      - "15672:15672" # Management UI
    environment:
      RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_USER: app
      RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_PASS: app_secret
      RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_VHOST: /app
      # Prevent RabbitMQ from consuming all host memory in containers
      RABBITMQ_VM_MEMORY_HIGH_WATERMARK: "0.6" # 60% limit
    volumes:
      - rabbitmq_data:/var/lib/rabbitmq # Persists queues, exchanges, and messages
    networks:
      - rabbitmq_net
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "rabbitmq-diagnostics", "check_port_connectivity"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

volumes:
  rabbitmq_data: # Named volume ensures data survives `docker compose down`

networks:
  rabbitmq_net:
    driver: bridge
```

**Key Details:**
*   **Persistent Volume (`rabbitmq_data`)**: Without this, all queues and messages are lost when the container stops.
*   **Fixed Hostname (`my-rabbit`)**: RabbitMQ uses the hostname as part of its node identifier. Changing it can make persisted data unreadable.
*   **Memory Watermark**: In containers, RabbitMQ can misjudge the host's memory. Setting an absolute limit (or a relative fraction) prevents OOM crashes.

Start the broker with:
```bash
docker compose up -d
```
Access the Management UI at `http://localhost:15672` with `app` / `app_secret`.

---

### 🔀 Step 2: Mastering Exchange Types (with Code)

Now that the broker is running, you can implement the four exchange types. The **Docker Compose network** allows your Java applications (whether running on the host or in other containers) to connect using the hostname `localhost` (if exposed) or the service name `rabbitmq` (if containerized together).

| Exchange Type | Routing Mechanism | Use Case |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Direct** | Exact routing key match | Task queues, point-to-point |
| **Fanout** | Broadcast to all bound queues | Notifications, cache invalidation |
| **Topic** | Pattern matching (`order.*.eu`) | Event filtering by region/severity |
| **Headers** | Matches on message header attributes | Complex routing rules |

**Spring Boot Implementation (Declaring Exchanges):**

```java
@Configuration
public class ExchangeConfig {

    // 1. Direct Exchange
    @Bean
    public DirectExchange directExchange() {
        return new DirectExchange("app.direct.exchange");
    }

    // 2. Fanout Exchange
    @Bean
    public FanoutExchange fanoutExchange() {
        return new FanoutExchange("app.fanout.exchange");
    }

    // 3. Topic Exchange
    @Bean
    public TopicExchange topicExchange() {
        return new TopicExchange("app.topic.exchange");
    }

    // 4. Headers Exchange
    @Bean
    public HeadersExchange headersExchange() {
        return new HeadersExchange("app.headers.exchange");
    }
}
```

**Pure Java Implementation (Publishing to a Topic Exchange):**

```java
Channel channel = connection.createChannel();
channel.exchangeDeclare("app.topic.exchange", BuiltinExchangeType.TOPIC);

// Routing key pattern: "order.created.eu"
String routingKey = "order.created.eu";
String message = "New order from Europe";
channel.basicPublish("app.topic.exchange", routingKey, null, message.getBytes());
```

---

### 🛡️ Step 3: Ensuring Delivery (Publisher Confirms & Returns)

A message is not truly sent until the broker **confirms** it has taken responsibility. Additionally, if a message cannot be routed to any queue, it should be **returned** to you rather than silently dropped.

**Spring Boot Configuration (`application.yml`):**

```yaml
spring:
  rabbitmq:
    host: localhost
    port: 5672
    username: app
    password: app_secret
    virtual-host: /app
    publisher-confirm-type: correlated # Enables async confirms
    publisher-returns: true            # Enables returns for unroutable messages
    template:
      mandatory: true                  # Required for returns to fire
```

**Spring Boot Callback Implementation:**

```java
@Configuration
public class RabbitTemplateConfig {

    @Autowired
    private RabbitTemplate rabbitTemplate;

    @PostConstruct
    public void configureTemplate() {
        // Confirm Callback: Did the broker accept the message?
        rabbitTemplate.setConfirmCallback((correlationData, ack, cause) -> {
            if (!ack) {
                System.err.println("Message NACKed by broker. Cause: " + cause);
                // Implement retry logic or alerting here
            } else {
                System.out.println("Message confirmed by broker.");
            }
        });

        // Return Callback: Was the message routable to a queue?
        rabbitTemplate.setReturnsCallback(returned -> {
            System.err.println("Message returned (unroutable): " + returned);
            // Log, send to a parking queue, or alert
        });
    }
}
```

**Pure Java Implementation:**

```java
Channel channel = connection.createChannel();
channel.confirmSelect(); // Enable publisher confirms

// Listen for confirms
channel.addConfirmListener(
    (sequenceNumber, multiple) -> System.out.println("Confirmed: " + sequenceNumber),
    (sequenceNumber, multiple) -> System.err.println("Nacked: " + sequenceNumber)
);

// Listen for returns
channel.addReturnListener(returned -> 
    System.err.println("Returned: " + returned.getReplyText())
);

// Publish with the `mandatory` flag set to true
channel.basicPublish("app.direct.exchange", "bad.routing.key", true, null, "Test".getBytes());
```

---

### ⚙️ Step 4: Consumer Reliability (Manual Ack & Prefetch)

Auto-acknowledgment is dangerous because a message is lost if the consumer crashes mid-processing. **Manual acknowledgment** gives you control, while **prefetch** prevents a consumer from being overwhelmed.

**Spring Boot Configuration (`application.yml`):**

```yaml
spring:
  rabbitmq:
    listener:
      simple:
        acknowledge-mode: manual
        prefetch: 10 # Fetch up to 10 unacknowledged messages at a time
```

**Spring Boot Listener with Manual Ack:**

```java
@Component
public class ReliableConsumer {

    @RabbitListener(queues = "app.direct.queue")
    public void handleMessage(
            String message,
            @Header(AmqpHeaders.DELIVERY_TAG) long deliveryTag,
            Channel channel) throws IOException {

        try {
            // ... business logic ...
            System.out.println("Processed: " + message);
            channel.basicAck(deliveryTag, false); // Success
        } catch (RetryableException e) {
            // Requeue for another attempt
            channel.basicNack(deliveryTag, false, true);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            // Reject without requeue (will go to DLQ if configured)
            channel.basicNack(deliveryTag, false, false);
        }
    }
}
```

**Pure Java Implementation:**

```java
channel.basicQos(10); // Prefetch limit

channel.basicConsume("app.direct.queue", false, (consumerTag, delivery) -> {
    long tag = delivery.getEnvelope().getDeliveryTag();
    try {
        // ... process ...
        channel.basicAck(tag, false);
    } catch (Exception e) {
        channel.basicNack(tag, false, true); // Requeue on failure
    }
}, consumerTag -> {});
```

---

### 🪦 Step 5: Handling Failures (Dead Letter Queue)

A **Dead Letter Exchange (DLX)** catches messages that are rejected (with `requeue=false`), expire, or exceed queue length limits. The Docker Compose setup is unchanged; the DLX is configured at the application level.

**Spring Boot DLQ Configuration:**

```java
@Configuration
public class DlqConfig {

    public static final String PRIMARY_QUEUE = "app.primary.queue";
    public static final String DLQ = "app.dead.letter.queue";
    public static final String DLX = "app.dlx.exchange";

    @Bean
    public Queue primaryQueue() {
        return QueueBuilder.durable(PRIMARY_QUEUE)
                .deadLetterExchange(DLX)
                .deadLetterRoutingKey("dlq.key")
                .build();
    }

    @Bean
    public Queue deadLetterQueue() {
        return QueueBuilder.durable(DLQ).build();
    }

    @Bean
    public DirectExchange deadLetterExchange() {
        return new DirectExchange(DLX);
    }

    @Bean
    public Binding dlqBinding() {
        return BindingBuilder.bind(deadLetterQueue())
                .to(deadLetterExchange())
                .with("dlq.key");
    }
}
```

**Pure Java DLQ Declaration:**

```java
Map<String, Object> args = new HashMap<>();
args.put("x-dead-letter-exchange", "app.dlx.exchange");
args.put("x-dead-letter-routing-key", "dlq.key");

channel.queueDeclare("app.primary.queue", true, false, false, args);
```

A powerful pattern is to add a **listener on the DLQ** that implements a retry limit before moving the message to a final "parking lot" queue for manual inspection.

---

### 💎 Summary: How It All Fits Together

| Layer | Component | Role in the Docker Compose Stack |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Infrastructure** | RabbitMQ container | Provides the broker, Management UI, and persistent volume. |
| **Routing** | Exchanges | Directs messages based on keys or headers. |
| **Producer Reliability** | Confirms & Returns | Ensures the broker accepted the message and it was routable. |
| **Consumer Reliability** | Manual Ack & Prefetch | Prevents message loss on consumer failure and controls flow. |
| **Failure Handling** | DLX / DLQ | Captures and isolates messages that cannot be processed. |

With this Docker Compose foundation, you can now run both your Spring Boot and pure Java applications against the same broker, observing the behavior of confirms, manual acks, and DLQs in real time through the Management UI.



<!-- SOURCE: 4.md -->
# File: 4.md

Moving beyond reliability primitives, the next step is designing systems that are **resilient to failure and duplicates**. This covers surviving broker restarts, handling duplicate deliveries safely, and controlling the order in which messages are processed.

---

### 💾 Step 6: Message Persistence & Quorum Queues

Publisher confirms guarantee the broker *received* a message. Persistence guarantees it survives a broker **restart or crash**. This requires **three things to align**: a durable exchange, a durable queue, and a persistent message.

**The Three Pillars of Persistence**

| Layer | Configuration | Why It Matters |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Exchange** | `durable=true` | The routing metadata survives a broker restart. |
| **Queue** | `durable=true` | The queue definition and its messages survive a restart. |
| **Message** | `deliveryMode = PERSISTENT` (2) | The message body is written to disk, not just memory. |

**Spring Boot: Durable Queue & Persistent Message**

Spring AMQP declares exchanges and queues as durable by default when using `QueueBuilder.durable()`. For the **message itself**, you must set the delivery mode explicitly, typically via a `MessagePostProcessor` so it applies to every send.

```java
@Configuration
public class PersistenceConfig {

    // Durable queue (and quorum queue discussed below)
    @Bean
    public Queue durableQueue() {
        return QueueBuilder.durable("persistent.queue").build();
    }

    // Configure the template to make every message persistent
    @Bean
    public RabbitTemplate rabbitTemplate(ConnectionFactory connectionFactory) {
        RabbitTemplate template = new RabbitTemplate(connectionFactory);
        template.setBeforePublishPostProcessors(message -> {
            message.getMessageProperties()
                   .setDeliveryMode(MessageDeliveryMode.PERSISTENT);
            return message;
        });
        return template;
    }
}
```

**Pure Java: Persistent Message**

```java
AMQP.BasicProperties props = new AMQP.BasicProperties.Builder()
        .deliveryMode(2) // 2 = PERSISTENT
        .build();
channel.basicPublish("exchange", "key", props, message.getBytes());
```

**Upgrading to Quorum Queues for High Availability**

For production, **quorum queues** are the recommended durable queue type. They replicate data across multiple RabbitMQ nodes using the Raft consensus algorithm, protecting against single-node failure.

In Spring Boot, declare a quorum queue by chaining `.quorum()`:

```java
@Bean
public Queue quorumQueue() {
    return QueueBuilder.durable("orders.processing")
            .quorum() // Forces durable=true and disables exclusive/auto-delete
            .build();
}
```

> **Important**: Your RabbitMQ cluster must have **at least 3 nodes** for quorum queues to function correctly. The single-node Docker Compose setup from earlier is sufficient for learning, but production requires a cluster.

---

### 🔁 Step 7: Idempotent Consumers (Handling Duplicates)

In any at-least-once delivery system, duplicates are inevitable. A consumer may process a message successfully but crash **before** sending the `basicAck`. When it restarts, the broker redelivers the message. The solution is to make the consumer **idempotent**: processing the same message twice should have the same effect as processing it once.

**The Standard Pattern: Deduplication Key**

1.  The producer assigns a **globally unique `messageId`** to every message.
2.  The consumer checks if this `messageId` has been seen before (in Redis, a database, or a local cache).
3.  If it is new, process the message and **atomically record** the `messageId`.
4.  If it already exists, **acknowledge and discard** the duplicate.

**Producer: Injecting a Unique `messageId`**

```java
@Bean
public MessageConverter messageConverter() {
    Jackson2JsonMessageConverter converter = new Jackson2JsonMessageConverter();
    converter.setCreateMessageIds(true); // Auto-generates a UUID per message
    return converter;
}
```

**Consumer: Idempotency Check with Redis**

A common and performant approach is to use Redis `SETNX` (set-if-not-exists) with a TTL.

```java
@Service
public class IdempotentConsumer {

    private final StringRedisTemplate redisTemplate;

    public IdempotentConsumer(StringRedisTemplate redisTemplate) {
        this.redisTemplate = redisTemplate;
    }

    @RabbitListener(queues = "persistent.queue")
    public void consume(Message message, Channel channel,
                         @Header(AmqpHeaders.DELIVERY_TAG) long tag) throws IOException {
        String messageId = message.getMessageProperties().getMessageId();

        // SETNX with a 24-hour TTL: returns true only if the key was newly set
        Boolean isNew = redisTemplate.opsForValue()
                .setIfAbsent("msg:id:" + messageId, "1", Duration.ofHours(24));

        if (Boolean.FALSE.equals(isNew)) {
            System.out.println("Duplicate detected, skipping: " + messageId);
            channel.basicAck(tag, false); // Acknowledge without processing
            return;
        }

        try {
            // ... business logic ...
            channel.basicAck(tag, false);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            // If processing fails, remove the idempotency key so a retry can proceed
            redisTemplate.delete("msg:id:" + messageId);
            channel.basicNack(tag, false, true);
        }
    }
}
```

> **Database alternative**: If Redis is unavailable, a **unique index** on a `processed_messages` table provides the same guarantee. Insert the `messageId` in the same transaction as the business logic; a `DuplicateKeyException` indicates a duplicate.

---

### ⏳ Step 8: Delayed Retry with TTL + Dead Letter Queue

A simple `basicNack` with `requeue=true` causes an **immediate** redelivery, which can hammer a failing consumer in a tight loop. A **delayed retry** pattern inserts a controlled wait between attempts.

**How It Works**

1.  The primary queue rejects the message **without requeue** (`requeue=false`).
2.  The message is dead-lettered to a **retry queue** that has a **TTL** (Time-To-Live).
3.  When the TTL expires, the message is dead-lettered **again**, back to the primary queue.
4.  After a maximum number of retries, the message is routed to a final **parking lot DLQ** for human inspection.

**Spring Boot Configuration**

```java
@Configuration
public class RetryDlqConfig {

    public static final String PRIMARY_QUEUE = "retry.primary.queue";
    public static final String RETRY_QUEUE   = "retry.delay.queue";
    public static final String PARKING_QUEUE = "retry.parking.queue";

    // Primary queue: on rejection, send to the retry (delay) queue
    @Bean
    public Queue primaryQueue() {
        return QueueBuilder.durable(PRIMARY_QUEUE)
                .deadLetterExchange("")
                .deadLetterRoutingKey(RETRY_QUEUE)
                .build();
    }

    // Delay queue: TTL of 5 seconds, then dead-letter back to the primary queue
    @Bean
    public Queue retryQueue() {
        return QueueBuilder.durable(RETRY_QUEUE)
                .ttl(5000) // 5-second delay
                .deadLetterExchange("")
                .deadLetterRoutingKey(PRIMARY_QUEUE)
                .build();
    }

    @Bean
    public Queue parkingQueue() {
        return QueueBuilder.durable(PARKING_QUEUE).build();
    }
}
```

**Consumer with Retry Count Tracking**

Use the `x-death` header (RabbitMQ's built-in dead-letter counter) to decide when to stop retrying.

```java
@RabbitListener(queues = RetryDlqConfig.PRIMARY_QUEUE)
public void consume(String message, Channel channel,
                    @Header(AmqpHeaders.DELIVERY_TAG) long tag,
                    @Header(name = "x-death", required = false) List<Map<String, Object>> xDeath)
        throws IOException {

    long retryCount = 0;
    if (xDeath != null) {
        retryCount = ((Number) xDeath.get(0).get("count")).longValue();
    }

    try {
        // ... business logic ...
        channel.basicAck(tag, false);
    } catch (Exception e) {
        if (retryCount < 3) {
            // Reject -> goes to retry queue (5s delay) -> back to primary
            channel.basicNack(tag, false, false);
        } else {
            // Exhausted retries -> route to parking queue for manual review
            channel.basicPublish("", RetryDlqConfig.PARKING_QUEUE, null,
                    message.getBytes());
            channel.basicAck(tag, false);
        }
    }
}
```

> **Caveat — Head-of-Line Blocking**: With a **single** TTL queue, RabbitMQ's FIFO nature means a message at the **head** with a long TTL blocks later messages with shorter TTLs from expiring. For precise per-message delays, use the `rabbitmq_delayed_message_exchange` plugin instead.

---

### 🎯 Step 9: Priority Queues

When some messages are objectively more urgent than others (e.g., high-value customer orders), a **priority queue** ensures they jump ahead of lower-priority messages already waiting.

**Configuration**: Set `x-max-priority` on the queue, and assign a `priority` on each message.

```java
@Bean
public Queue priorityQueue() {
    return QueueBuilder.durable("priority.queue")
            .maxPriority(10) // Allowed range: 0–255; avoid very high values (CPU/memory cost)
            .build();
}
```

**Sending with a Priority**

```java
public void sendWithPriority(String message, int priority) {
    rabbitTemplate.convertAndSend("priority.queue", message, msg -> {
        msg.getMessageProperties().setPriority(priority);
        return msg;
    });
}
```

**Pure Java**

```java
Map<String, Object> args = new HashMap<>();
args.put("x-max-priority", 10);
channel.queueDeclare("priority.queue", true, false, false, args);

AMQP.BasicProperties props = new AMQP.BasicProperties.Builder()
        .priority(9) // Higher number = consumed first
        .build();
channel.basicPublish("", "priority.queue", props, message.getBytes());
```

> **Best practice**: Keep `x-max-priority` small (10 is typical). A large range increases RabbitMQ's internal sorting overhead without practical benefit.

---

### 🔄 Step 10: RPC (Request-Reply) over RabbitMQ

Although RabbitMQ is fundamentally asynchronous, Spring AMQP provides a clean abstraction for **synchronous RPC** using the `convertSendAndReceive` method.

**How It Works**: Spring automatically creates a **callback queue** for the client, sets the `replyTo` and `correlationId` message properties, and matches the response back to the correct request.

**Client (Synchronous Call)**

```java
@Service
public class RpcClient {

    private final RabbitTemplate rabbitTemplate;

    public RpcClient(RabbitTemplate rabbitTemplate) {
        this.rabbitTemplate = rabbitTemplate;
    }

    public Integer getFibonacci(int n) {
        // Blocks until the server responds (or times out)
        Integer result = (Integer) rabbitTemplate.convertSendAndReceive(
                "rpc.exchange", "rpc.fib", n);
        return result;
    }
}
```

**Server (Listener that Returns a Value)**

```java
@RabbitListener(queues = "rpc.fib.queue")
public Integer computeFibonacci(int n) {
    // The return value is automatically sent back to the client's callback queue
    return fib(n);
}

private int fib(int n) {
    return n <= 1 ? n : fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}
```

> **Use RPC sparingly**. As the RabbitMQ tutorial notes, RPC can make an asynchronous system feel synchronous and introduce hidden coupling. Prefer **async pipelines** (events with separate response queues) when the result is not needed immediately.

---

### 🐳 Step 11: Spring Boot Docker Compose Support (Dev Convenience)

You already have a `docker-compose.yml`. Spring Boot 3.1+ can **automatically detect and start it** when your application runs, removing the need to manually run `docker compose up` during development.

**1. Add the Dependency**

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-docker-compose</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
    <optional>true</optional>
</dependency>
```

**2. Keep Your `docker-compose.yml` in the Project Root**

When you run the Spring Boot application:
- Spring Boot searches for `compose.yml` / `docker-compose.yml`.
- It runs `docker compose up` automatically.
- It creates a `ConnectionDetails` bean pointing to the RabbitMQ container, so you can **remove** `spring.rabbitmq.host/port/username/password` from `application.yml` (they are auto-configured).
- On shutdown, it runs `docker compose stop`.

> **Remove this dependency before deploying to production**; it is a development-only convenience.

---

### 💎 Summary: What You Can Now Build

| Pattern | Problem It Solves | Key Mechanism |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Persistence + Quorum** | Broker restart loses messages | `durable` + `deliveryMode=2` + `.quorum()` |
| **Idempotency** | Duplicate delivery causes double-processing | Unique `messageId` + Redis `SETNX` / DB unique index |
| **Delayed Retry + DLQ** | Immediate requeue hammers a failing consumer | TTL retry queue + `x-death` count + parking queue |
| **Priority Queue** | Urgent messages wait behind bulk messages | `x-max-priority` + per-message `priority` |
| **RPC** | Synchronous request-response over an async broker | `convertSendAndReceive` + `replyTo`/`correlationId` |

A natural next topic would be the **Outbox Pattern** for guaranteeing that a database write and a message publish happen atomically—a common requirement when RabbitMQ is part of a larger transactional workflow.

## 6.16.0 (2017-02-23)

### :rocket: New Feature

***ESTree*** compatibility as plugin ([#277](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/277)) (Daniel Tschinder)

We finally introduce a new compatibility layer for ESTree. To put babylon into ESTree-compatible mode the new plugin `estree` can be enabled. In this mode the parser will output an AST that is compliant to the specs of [ESTree](https://github.com/estree/estree/)

We highly recommend everyone who uses babylon outside of babel to use this plugin. This will make it much easier for users to switch between different ESTree-compatible parsers. We so far tested several projects with different parsers and exchanged their parser to babylon and in nearly all cases it worked out of the box. Some other estree-compatible parsers include `acorn`, `esprima`, `espree`, `flow-parser`, etc.

To enable `estree` mode simply add the plugin in the config:
```json
{
  "plugins": [ "estree" ]
}
```

If you want to migrate your project from non-ESTree mode to ESTree, have a look at our [Readme](https://github.com/babel/babylon/#output), where all deviations are mentioned.

Add a parseExpression public method ([#213](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/213)) (jeromew)

Babylon exports a new function to parse a single expression

```js
import { parseExpression } from 'babylon';

const ast = parseExpression('x || y && z', options);
```

The returned AST will only consist of the expression. The options are the same as for `parse()`

Add startLine option ([#346](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/346)) (Raphael Mu)

A new option was added to babylon allowing to change the initial linenumber for the first line which is usually `1`.
Changing this for example to `100` will make line `1` of the input source to be marked as line `100`, line `2` as `101`, line `3` as `102`, ...

Function predicate declaration ([#103](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/103)) (Panagiotis Vekris)

Added support for function predicates which flow introduced in version 0.33.0

```js
declare function is_number(x: mixed): boolean %checks(typeof x === "number");
```

Allow imports in declare module ([#315](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/315)) (Daniel Tschinder)

Added support for imports within module declarations which flow introduced in version 0.37.0

```js
declare module "C" {
  import type { DT } from "D";
  declare export type CT = { D: DT };
}
```

### :eyeglasses: Spec Compliance

Forbid semicolons after decorators in classes ([#352](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/352)) (Kevin Gibbons)

This example now correctly throws an error when there is a semicolon after the decorator:

```js
class A {
@a;
foo(){}
}
```

Keywords are not allowed as local specifier ([#307](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/307)) (Daniel Tschinder)

Using keywords in imports is not allowed anymore:

```js
import { default } from "foo";
import { a as debugger } from "foo";
```

Do not allow overwritting of primitive types ([#314](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/314)) (Daniel Tschinder)

In flow it is now forbidden to overwrite the primitive types `"any"`, `"mixed"`, `"empty"`, `"bool"`, `"boolean"`, `"number"`, `"string"`, `"void"` and `"null"` with your own type declaration.

Disallow import type { type a } from … ([#305](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/305)) (Daniel Tschinder)

The following code now correctly throws an error

```js
import type { type a } from "foo";
```

Don't parse class properties without initializers when classProperties is disabled and Flow is enabled ([#300](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/300)) (Andrew Levine)

Ensure that you enable the `classProperties` plugin in order to enable correct parsing of class properties. Prior to this version it was possible to parse them by enabling the `flow` plugin but this was not intended the behaviour.

If you enable the flow plugin you can only define the type of the class properties, but not initialize them.

Fix export default async function to be FunctionDeclaration ([#324](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/324)) (Daniel Tschinder)

Parsing the following code now returns a `FunctionDeclaration` AST node instead of `FunctionExpression`.

```js
export default async function bar() {};
```

## 6.15.0 (2017-01-10)

### :eyeglasses: Spec Compliance

Add support for Flow shorthand import type ([#267](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/267)) (Jeff Morrison)

This change implements flows new shorthand import syntax
and where previously you had to write this code:

```js
import {someValue} from "blah";
import type {someType} from "blah";
import typeof {someOtherValue} from "blah";
```

you can now write it like this:

```js
import {
  someValue,
  type someType,
  typeof someOtherValue,
} from "blah";
```

For more information look at [this](https://github.com/facebook/flow/pull/2890) pull request.

flow: allow leading pipes in all positions ([#256](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/256)) (Vladimir Kurchatkin)

This change now allows a leading pipe everywhere types can be used:
```js
var f = (x): | 1 | 2 => 1;
```

Throw error when exporting non-declaration ([#241](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/241)) (Kai Cataldo)

Previously babylon parsed the following exports, although they are not valid:
```js
export typeof foo;
export new Foo();
export function() {};
export for (;;);
export while(foo);
```

## v6.11.3 (2016-10-01)

### :eyeglasses: Spec Compliance

Add static errors for object rest (#149) ([@danez](https://github.com/danez))

> https://github.com/sebmarkbage/ecmascript-rest-spread

Object rest copies the *rest* of properties from the right hand side `obj` starting from the left to right.

```js
let { x, y, ...z } =  { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 };
// x = 1
// y = 2
// z = { z: 3 }
```

#### New Syntax Errors:

**SyntaxError**: The rest element has to be the last element when destructuring (1:10)
```bash
> 1 | let { ...x, y, z } = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3};
    |           ^
# Previous behavior:
# x = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 }
# y = 2
# z = 3
```

Before, this was just a more verbose way of shallow copying `obj` since it doesn't actually do what you think.

**SyntaxError**: Cannot have multiple rest elements when destructuring (1:13)

```bash
> 1 | let { x, ...y, ...z } = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3};
    |              ^
# Previous behavior:
# x = 1
# y = { y: 2, z: 3 }
# z = { y: 2, z: 3 }
```

Before y and z would just be the same value anyway so there is no reason to need to have both.

**SyntaxError**: A trailing comma is not permitted after the rest element (1:16)

```js
let { x, y, ...z, } = obj;
```

The rationale for this is that the use case for trailing comma is that you can add something at the end without affecting the line above. Since a RestProperty always has to be the last property it doesn't make sense.

---

get / set are valid property names in default assignment (#142) ([@jezell](https://github.com/jezell))

```js
// valid
function something({ set = null, get = null }) {}
```

```js
export default {};
export default function() {};

// `Foo` has already been exported. Exported identifiers must be unique. (2:0)
export { Foo };
export class Foo {};
```

### New Feature (Syntax)

- Add support for computed class property names ([#121](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/121)) @motiz88

```js
// AST
interface ClassProperty <: Node {
  type: "ClassProperty";
  key: Identifier;
  value: Expression;
  computed: boolean; // added
}
```

```js
// with "plugins": ["classProperties"]
class Foo {
  [x]
  ['y']
}

class Bar {
  [p]
  [m] () {}
}
 ```

### Bug Fix

- Fix `static` property falling through in the declare class Flow AST ([#135](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/135)) @danharper

```js

    a: number;
    static b: number; // static

}
```

### Polish

- Rephrase "assigning/binding to rvalue" errors to include context ([#119](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/119)) @motiz88

```js

// Now:
// Invalid left-hand side in assignment expression (1:0)
3 = 4

// Invalid left-hand side in for-in statement (1:5)

```

### Internal

- Add semver note to changelog ([#131](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/131)) @hzoo

## 6.10.0 (2016-09-19)

> We plan to include some spec compliance bugs in patch versions. An example was the multiple default exports issue.

### Spec Compliance

* Implement ES2016 check for simple parameter list in strict mode ([#106](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/106)) (Timothy Gu)

> It is a Syntax Error if ContainsUseStrict of FunctionBody is true and IsSimpleParameterList of FormalParameters is false. https://tc39.github.io/ecma262/2016/#sec-function-definitions-static-semantics-early-errors

More Context: [tc39-notes](https://github.com/rwaldron/tc39-notes/blob/master/es7/2015-07/july-29.md#611-the-scope-of-use-strict-with-respect-to-destructuring-in-parameter-lists)

For example:

```js
// this errors because it uses destructuring and default parameters
// in a function with a "use strict" directive
function a([ option1, option2 ] = []) {
  "use strict";
}
 ```

The solution would be to use a top level "use strict" or to remove the destructuring or default parameters when using a function + "use strict" or to.

### New Feature

* Exact object type annotations for Flow plugin ([#104](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/104)) (Basil Hosmer)

Added to flow in https://github.com/facebook/flow/commit/c710c40aa2a115435098d6c0dfeaadb023cd39b8

Looks like:

```js
var a : {| x: number, y: string |} = { x: 0, y: 'foo' };
```

### Bug Fixes

* Include `typeParameter` location in `ArrowFunctionExpression` ([#126](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/126)) (Daniel Tschinder)
* Error on invalid flow type annotation with default assignment ([#122](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/122)) (Dan Harper)
* Fix Flow return types on arrow functions ([#124](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/124)) (Dan Harper)

* Fix Contributing guidelines [skip ci] (Daniel Tschinder)

## 6.9.2 (2016-09-09)

The only change is to remove the `babel-runtime` dependency by compiling with Babel's ES2015 loose mode. So using babylon standalone should be smaller.

## 6.9.1 (2016-08-23)

This release contains mainly small bugfixes but also updates babylons default mode to es2017. The features for `exponentiationOperator`, `asyncFunctions` and `trailingFunctionCommas` which previously needed to be activated via plugin are now enabled by default and the plugins are now no-ops.

#### New Feature

> [Method Parameter Decorators](https://goo.gl/8MmCMG) is now a TC39 [stage 0 proposal](https://github.com/tc39/ecma262/blob/master/stage0.md).

Examples:


Example:

```js

  for await (let x of y);
}
```
