# File: 9.md

# جلسه ۹: پروژه‌های عملی (جمع‌بندی جلسات ۱ تا ۸)

## 🎯 اهداف این جلسه
در این جلسه همه مفاهیم قبلی را در قالب **سه پروژه کامل** به کار می‌گیریم:

1. **اسلایدر تصاویر** — انیمیشن + رویداد + پیمایش + زنجیره‌سازی
2. **اعتبارسنجی فرم** — رویدادها + `val()` + کلاس‌ها + `prop()`
3. **لیست کارها با AJAX** — دستکاری DOM + تفویض رویداد + AJAX + Promise

در پایان هر پروژه، بخش «چه چیزی از کدام جلسه استفاده شد» را می‌بینی تا اتصال مفاهیم را حس کنی.

---

# 🖼️ پروژه ۱: اسلایدر تصاویر

## هدف
نمایش یک اسلایدر با دکمه‌های قبلی/بعدی، نقطه‌های ناوبری (dots)، و چرخش خودکار (auto-play).

## ساختار HTML
```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="fa" dir="rtl">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>اسلایدر jQuery</title>
  <script src="https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.7.1.min.js"></script>
  <style>
    * { box-sizing: border-box; }
    body { font-family: Tahoma, sans-serif; background: #f4f4f4; }

    .slider {
      position: relative;
      width: 600px;
      height: 350px;
      margin: 40px auto;
      overflow: hidden;
      border-radius: 12px;
      box-shadow: 0 4px 20px rgba(0,0,0,0.15);
    }

    .slider .slide {
      position: absolute;
      inset: 0;
      opacity: 0;
      transition: opacity 0.6s;
    }

    .slider .slide.active { opacity: 1; }

    .slider .slide img {
      width: 100%;
      height: 100%;
      object-fit: cover;
      display: block;
    }

    .slider .caption {
      position: absolute;
      bottom: 0;
      right: 0; left: 0;
      background: rgba(0,0,0,0.55);
      color: #fff;
      padding: 10px 16px;
      font-size: 16px;
    }

    .controls {
      position: absolute;
      top: 50%;
      transform: translateY(-50%);
      width: 100%;
      display: flex;
      justify-content: space-between;
      padding: 0 10px;
      pointer-events: none;
    }

    .controls button {
      pointer-events: auto;
      width: 40px; height: 40px;
      border: none; border-radius: 50%;
      background: rgba(255,255,255,0.8);
      cursor: pointer;
      font-size: 20px;
      transition: background 0.2s;
    }
    .controls button:hover { background: #fff; }

    .dots {
      position: absolute;
      bottom: 12px;
      left: 50%;
      transform: translateX(-50%);
      display: flex;
      gap: 8px;
    }

    .dots span {
      width: 12px; height: 12px;
      border-radius: 50%;
      background: rgba(255,255,255,0.5);
      cursor: pointer;
      transition: background 0.2s, transform 0.2s;
    }
    .dots span.active { background: #fff; transform: scale(1.25); }
  </style>
</head>
<body>

  <div class="slider" id="slider">
    <div class="slide active">
      <img src="https://picsum.photos/id/1015/600/350" alt="">
      <div class="caption">کوهستان — تصویر ۱</div>
    </div>
    <div class="slide">
      <img src="https://picsum.photos/id/1025/600/350" alt="">
      <div class="caption">سگ — تصویر ۲</div>
    </div>
    <div class="slide">
      <img src="https://picsum.photos/id/1035/600/350" alt="">
      <div class="caption">جاده — تصویر ۳</div>
    </div>

    <div class="controls">
      <button class="prev">‹</button>
      <button class="next">›</button>
    </div>

    <div class="dots"></div>
  </div>

  <script>
  $(function() {
    var $slides = $("#slider .slide");
    var $dots   = $("#slider .dots");
    var total   = $slides.length;
    var current = 0;
    var timer   = null;
    var AUTOPLAY = 4000;

    // ساخت نقطه‌های ناوبری بر اساس تعداد اسلایدها
    $slides.each(function(i) {
      $("<span>")
        .attr("data-index", i)
        .toggleClass("active", i === 0)
        .appendTo($dots);
    });

    function goTo(index) {
      // نرمال‌سازی ایندکس (چرخش دایره‌ای)
      current = (index + total) % total;

      $slides.removeClass("active").eq(current).addClass("active");
      $dots.find("span").removeClass("active").eq(current).addClass("active");
    }

    function next() { goTo(current + 1); }
    function prev() { goTo(current - 1); }

    function startAuto() {
      stopAuto();
      timer = setInterval(next, AUTOPLAY);
    }
    function stopAuto() {
      if (timer) { clearInterval(timer); timer = null; }
    }

    // رویداد دکمه‌ها
    $("#slider .next").on("click", function() { next(); startAuto(); });
    $("#slider .prev").on("click", function() { prev(); startAuto(); });

    // تفویض رویداد برای dots
    $dots.on("click", "span", function() {
      var i = $(this).data("index");
      goTo(i);
      startAuto();
    });

    // توقف هنگام hover (تجربه بهتر)
    $("#slider")
      .on("mouseenter", stopAuto)
      .on("mouseleave", startAuto);

    // پشتیبانی از کلیدهای جهت‌دار
    $(document).on("keydown", function(e) {
      if (e.key === "ArrowLeft")  { next(); startAuto(); }
      if (e.key === "ArrowRight") { prev(); startAuto(); }
    });

    startAuto();
  });
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

## چه چیزی از کدام جلسه استفاده شد؟
| مفهوم | جلسه |
|---|---|
| `$(function(){})`، انتخابگرها | ۱ و ۲ |
| `on()`، `mouseenter`، `mouseleave`، تفویض رویداد | ۳ |
| `toggleClass`، `removeClass`، `addClass` | ۵ |
| `eq()`، `find()`، `each()` | ۶ و ۸ |
| `data()` | ۸ |
| زنجیره‌سازی | ۸ |

## ✍️ تمرین پروژه ۱
1. یک دکمه «توقف/پخش» اضافه کن که `autoplay` را کنترل کند.
2. به هر نقطه ناوبری یک tooltip ساده با `attr("title", ...)` بده.
3. تعداد اسلاید را به ۵ برسان و مطمئن شو چرخش دایره‌ای درست کار می‌کند.

---

# 📝 پروژه ۲: اعتبارسنجی فرم (Form Validation)

## هدف
فرم ثبت‌نام با اعتبارسنجی سمت کلاینت و پیام‌های خطای خط‌به‌خط.

## ساختار HTML
```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="fa" dir="rtl">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>اعتبارسنجی فرم</title>
  <script src="https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.7.1.min.js"></script>
  <style>
    * { box-sizing: border-box; }
    body { font-family: Tahoma, sans-serif; background: #eef2f7; padding: 30px; }

    .form-box {
      max-width: 420px;
      margin: 0 auto;
      background: #fff;
      padding: 26px;
      border-radius: 12px;
      box-shadow: 0 4px 20px rgba(0,0,0,0.08);
    }

    .field { margin-bottom: 16px; }

    .field label {
      display: block;
      margin-bottom: 6px;
      font-weight: bold;
      color: #333;
    }

    .field input {
      width: 100%;
      padding: 10px 12px;
      border: 2px solid #ddd;
      border-radius: 8px;
      font-size: 15px;
      transition: border-color 0.2s;
    }

    .field input:focus { outline: none; border-color: #4a90e2; }
    .field.error input  { border-color: #e74c3c; }
    .field.success input { border-color: #2ecc71; }

    .msg {
      font-size: 12px;
      margin-top: 6px;
      min-height: 16px;
      color: #e74c3c;
    }

    .field.success .msg { color: #2ecc71; }

    button[type="submit"] {
      width: 100%;
      padding: 12px;
      background: #4a90e2;
      color: #fff;
      border: none;
      border-radius: 8px;
      font-size: 16px;
      cursor: pointer;
      transition: background 0.2s;
    }
    button[type="submit"]:hover { background: #357ab8; }
    button[type="submit"]:disabled { background: #9bb; cursor: wait; }

    #result { text-align: center; margin-top: 16px; font-weight: bold; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>

  <form class="form-box" id="signupForm" novalidate>
    <div class="field" data-field="name">
      <label>نام</label>
      <input type="text" name="name" placeholder="حداقل ۳ حرف">
      <div class="msg"></div>
    </div>

    <div class="field" data-field="email">
      <label>ایمیل</label>
      <input type="text" name="email" placeholder="example@mail.com">
      <div class="msg"></div>
    </div>

    <div class="field" data-field="password">
      <label>رمز عبور</label>
      <input type="password" name="password" placeholder="حداقل ۶ کاراکتر">
      <div class="msg"></div>
    </div>

    <div class="field" data-field="age">
      <label>سن</label>
      <input type="text" name="age" placeholder="بین ۱۸ تا ۹۹">
      <div class="msg"></div>
    </div>

    <button type="submit">ثبت‌نام</button>
    <div id="result"></div>
  </form>

  <script>
  $(function() {
    // قواعد اعتبارسنجی هر فیلد
    var rules = {
      name: {
        validate: function(v) { return v.length >= 3; },
        message: "نام باید حداقل ۳ حرف باشد"
      },
      email: {
        validate: function(v) { return /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/.test(v); },
        message: "ایمیل معتبر نیست"
      },
      password: {
        validate: function(v) { return v.length >= 6; },
        message: "رمز عبور باید حداقل ۶ کاراکتر باشد"
      },
      age: {
        validate: function(v) { return /^\d+$/.test(v) && +v >= 18 && +v <= 99; },
        message: "سن باید عددی بین ۱۸ تا ۹۹ باشد"
      }
    };

    // اعتبارسنجی یک فیلد
    function validateField($field) {
      var key = $field.data("field");
      var value = $field.find("input").val().trim();
      var rule = rules[key];
      var ok = rule.validate(value);

      $field
        .toggleClass("error",   !ok)
        .toggleClass("success", ok)
        .find(".msg")
        .text(ok ? "" : rule.message);

      return ok;
    }

    // اعتبارسنجی روی blur (خروج از فیلد)
    $("#signupForm").on("blur", "input", function() {
      validateField($(this).closest(".field"));
    });

    // اعتبارسنجی زنده روی keyup (فقط اگر قبلاً خطا داشته)
    $("#signupForm").on("keyup", "input", function() {
      var $field = $(this).closest(".field");
      if ($field.hasClass("error")) validateField($field);
    });

    // ارسال فرم
    $("#signupForm").on("submit", function(event) {
      event.preventDefault();

      var allOk = true;
      $(this).find(".field").each(function() {
        if (!validateField($(this))) allOk = false;
      });

      if (!allOk) {
        $("#result").text("لطفاً خطاها را برطرف کن").css("color", "#e74c3c");
        return;
      }

      // شبیه‌سازی ارسال به سرور
      var $btn = $(this).find("button").prop("disabled", true).text("در حال ارسال…");

      var formData = $(this).serialize();

      // در پروژه واقعی: $.ajax(...)
      setTimeout(function() {
        $("#result").text("ثبت‌نام با موفقیت انجام شد ✅").css("color", "#2ecc71");
        $btn.prop("disabled", false).text("ثبت‌نام");
        console.log("داده ارسالی:", formData);
      }, 1000);
    });
  });
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

## چه چیزی از کدام جلسه استفاده شد؟
| مفهوم | جلسه |
|---|---|
| `$(function(){})`، انتخابگرها | ۱ و ۲ |
| `on()`، `blur`، `keyup`، `submit`، تفویض رویداد | ۳ |
| `val()`، `serialize()`، `prop("disabled")` | ۵ و ۷ |
| `toggleClass`، `hasClass`، `closest()`، `find()`، `each()` | ۵ و ۶ و ۸ |
| `preventDefault` | ۳ |

## ✍️ تمرین پروژه ۲
1. فیلد «تکرار رمز عبور» اضافه کن و بررسی کن با رمز اصلی یکسان باشد.
2. یک نشانگر قدرت رمز (ضعیف/متوسط/قوی) با رنگ زیر فیلد اضافه کن.
3. بعد از موفقیت، فرم را با `$form[0].reset()` خالی کن و کلاس‌های `success`/`error` را هم پاک کن.

---

# ✅ پروژه ۳: لیست کارها با AJAX

## هدف
آخرین پروژه، همه چیز را ترکیب می‌کند: دریافت داده با AJAX، ساخت DOM، تفویض رویداد، فیلتر، و ذخیره‌سازی در `localStorage`.

## ساختار HTML
```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="fa" dir="rtl">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>لیست کارها با AJAX</title>
  <script src="https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.7.1.min.js"></script>
  <style>
    * { box-sizing: border-box; }
    body { font-family: Tahoma, sans-serif; background: #f7f9fc; padding: 30px; }

    .wrap {
      max-width: 520px;
      margin: 0 auto;
      background: #fff;
      border-radius: 12px;
      padding: 22px;
      box-shadow: 0 4px 20px rgba(0,0,0,0.08);
    }

    h2 { margin-top: 0; text-align: center; color: #333; }

    .add-row { display: flex; gap: 8px; margin-bottom: 16px; }

    .add-row input {
      flex: 1;
      padding: 10px 12px;
      border: 2px solid #ddd;
      border-radius: 8px;
      font-size: 15px;
    }
    .add-row input:focus { outline: none; border-color: #4a90e2; }

    .add-row button {
      padding: 0 18px;
      background: #4a90e2;
      color: #fff;
      border: none;
      border-radius: 8px;
      font-size: 15px;
      cursor: pointer;
    }

    .filters {
      display: flex; gap: 6px;
      margin-bottom: 14px;
    }
    .filters button {
      flex: 1;
      padding: 8px;
      border: 1px solid #ddd;
      background: #fff;
      border-radius: 8px;
      cursor: pointer;
      transition: all 0.2s;
    }
    .filters button.active {
      background: #4a90e2; color: #fff; border-color: #4a90e2;
    }

    #todoList { list-style: none; padding: 0; margin: 0; }

    #todoList li {
      display: flex;
      align-items: center;
      gap: 10px;
      padding: 10px 12px;
      border-bottom: 1px solid #eee;
      transition: background 0.2s;
    }
    #todoList li:hover { background: #f9fbfd; }

    #todoList li.done .title {
      text-decoration: line-through;
      color: #999;
    }

    #todoList li .title { flex: 1; cursor: pointer; }

    #todoList li .del {
      background: #fff;
      border: 1px solid #e74c3c;
      color: #e74c3c;
      border-radius: 6px;
      padding: 4px 8px;
      cursor: pointer;
      font-size: 13px;
      transition: all 0.2s;
    }
    #todoList li .del:hover { background: #e74c3c; color: #fff; }

    .empty {
      text-align: center;
      color: #aaa;
      padding: 20px;
    }

    #loading {
      text-align: center;
      color: #4a90e2;
      font-size: 13px;
      min-height: 18px;
    }

    .footer {
      display: flex;
      justify-content: space-between;
      align-items: center;
      margin-top: 12px;
      font-size: 13px;
      color: #888;
    }
  </style>
</head>
<body>

  <div class="wrap">
    <h2>لیست کارها</h2>

    <div class="add-row">
      <input type="text" id="newTask" placeholder="کار جدید…">
      <button id="addBtn">افزودن</button>
    </div>

    <div class="filters">
      <button data-filter="all"    class="active">همه</button>
      <button data-filter="active">انجام‌نشده</button>
      <button data-filter="done">انجام‌شده</button>
    </div>

    <ul id="todoList"></ul>
    <div id="loading"></div>

    <div class="footer">
      <span id="count">۰ کار</span>
      <button id="clearDone" style="background:none;border:none;color:#e74c3c;cursor:pointer;">
        حذف انجام‌شده‌ها
      </button>
    </div>
  </div>

  <script>
  $(function() {
    var STORAGE_KEY = "my_todos";
    var $list = $("#todoList");
    var $loading = $("#loading");
    var filter = "all";

    // ---------- ابزار ----------
    function loadTodos() {
      var raw = localStorage.getItem(STORAGE_KEY);
      return raw ? JSON.parse(raw) : [];
    }

    function saveTodos(todos) {
      localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, JSON.stringify(todos));
    }

    function getTodos() { return loadTodos(); }

    // ---------- نمایش ----------
    function render() {
      var todos = getTodos();
      $list.empty();

      // اعمال فیلتر
      var filtered = todos.filter(function(t) {
        if (filter === "active") return !t.done;
        if (filter === "done")   return t.done;
        return true;
      });

      if (!filtered.length) {
        $list.append('<li class="empty">کاری برای نمایش نیست</li>');
      } else {
        filtered.forEach(function(t) {
          var $li = $("<li>")
            .attr("data-id", t.id)
            .toggleClass("done", t.done);

          $li.append(
            $("<span>").addClass("title").text(t.title),
            $("<button>").addClass("del").text("حذف")
          );

          $list.append($li);
        });
      }

      // شمارنده
      var doneCount = todos.filter(function(t) { return t.done; }).length;
      $("#count").text(todos.length + " کار · " + doneCount + " انجام‌شده");
    }

    // ---------- عملیات ----------
    function addTodo(title) {
      var todos = getTodos();
      todos.unshift({
        id: Date.now(),
        title: title,
        done: false
      });
      saveTodos(todos);
      render();
    }

    function removeTodo(id) {
      var todos = getTodos().filter(function(t) { return t.id !== id; });
      saveTodos(todos);
      render();
    }

    function toggleTodo(id) {
      var todos = getTodos();
      todos.forEach(function(t) {
        if (t.id === id) t.done = !t.done;
      });
      saveTodos(todos);
      render();
    }

    function clearDone() {
      var todos = getTodos().filter(function(t) { return !t.done; });
      saveTodos(todos);
      render();
    }

    // ---------- بارگذاری اولیه با AJAX ----------
    function bootstrap() {
      var todos = getTodos();

      if (todos.length) {
        render();
        return;
      }

      // اولین بار: داده نمونه از سرور بگیر
      $loading.text("در حال دریافت داده‌های اولیه…");

      $.getJSON("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos?_limit=5")
        .then(function(data) {
          var initial = data.map(function(t) {
            return { id: t.id, title: t.title, done: t.completed };
          });
          saveTodos(initial);
          render();
        })
        .catch(function() {
          $loading.text("دریافت داده‌ها ناموفق بود، خودت اضافه کن :)");
        })
        .always(function() {
          setTimeout(function() { $loading.text(""); }, 1500);
        });
    }

    // ---------- رویدادها ----------
    $("#addBtn").on("click", function() {
      var title = $("#newTask").val().trim();
      if (!title) return;
      addTodo(title);
      $("#newTask").val("").focus();
    });

    // Enter برای افزودن
    $("#newTask").on("keydown", function(e) {
      if (e.key === "Enter") $("#addBtn").trigger("click");
    });

    // تفویض رویداد روی لیست
    $list.on("click", ".title", function() {
      var id = $(this).closest("li").data("id");
      toggleTodo(id);
    });

    $list.on("click", ".del", function() {
      var id = $(this).closest("li").data("id");
      removeTodo(id);
    });

    // فیلترها
    $(".filters").on("click", "button", function() {
      filter = $(this).data("filter");
      $(this).addClass("active").siblings().removeClass("active");
      render();
    });

    // حذف انجام‌شده‌ها
    $("#clearDone").on("click", clearDone);

    // شروع
    bootstrap();
  });
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

## چه چیزی از کدام جلسه استفاده شد؟
| مفهوم | جلسه |
|---|---|
| انتخابگرها، `$(function(){})` | ۱ و ۲ |
| `on()`، `keydown`، تفویض رویداد | ۳ |
| `toggleClass`، `addClass`، `removeClass`، `text`، `empty`، `append`، `val` | ۵ |
| `closest()`، `find()`، `siblings()`، `each()` / `forEach` | ۶ و ۸ |
| `$.getJSON()`، Promise (`.then`، `.catch`، `.always`) | ۷ |
| `data()`، `attr()`، زنجیره‌سازی | ۵ و ۸ |

## ✍️ تمرین پروژه ۳
1. یک قابلیت «ویرایش» اضافه کن: با دوبار کلیک روی عنوان، آن را به یک input تبدیل کن و با Enter ذخیره کن (`dblclick`).
2. یک دکمه «پاک‌کردن همه» اضافه کن که پس از تأیید با `confirm()` همه را حذف کند.
3. یک جستجوی زنده بالای لیست اضافه کن (input با `keyup`) که لیست را بر اساس عنوان فیلتر کند.
4. با `$.ajax()` و `ajaxStart` / `ajaxStop`، هنگام دریافت داده اولیه یک spinner کوچک نمایش بده (به‌جای متن ساده).

---

## 🧭 مرور کامل مسیر یادگیری

| جلسه | مهارت اصلی |
|---|---|
| ۱ | راه‌اندازی و اولین کد |
| ۲ | انتخابگرها |
| ۳ | رویدادها و تفویض |
| ۴ | انیمیشن و افکت |
| ۵ | دستکاری DOM |
| ۶ | پیمایش |
| ۷ | AJAX و Promise |
| ۸ | زنجیره‌سازی، Deferred، پلاگین |
| ۹ | پروژه‌های ترکیبی ← **اکنون** |

---

## 📝 تکلیف نهایی (جمع‌بندی)

یک **پروژه مینی شخصی** بساز؛ مثلاً:
- **گالری تصاویر** با فیلتر دسته‌بندی (Ajax + DOM + رویداد)
- **لیست مخاطبین** با جستجو، افزودن/حذف، ذخیره در localStorage
- **داشبورد آب‌وهوا** با دریافت داده از یک API عمومی (`open-meteo.com` بدون کلید کار می‌کند)

الزامات:
1. حداقل از **سه مفهوم** از جلسات مختلف استفاده کن.
2. کد را **تمیز و کامنت‌گذاری‌شده** بنویس.
3. اگر عملیات ناهمگام دارد، از `.then()` / `.catch()` استفاده کن.
4. حداقل یک پلاگین کوچک سفارشی (مثل جلسه ۸) در پروژه‌ات داشته باش.

---

## ⏭️ جلسه بعد (اختیاری)
اگر خواستی، می‌توانیم برویم سراغ:
- **مقایسه jQuery با Vanilla JS مدرن** (چه زمانی jQuery لازم است، چه زمانی نه)
- **بهینه‌سازی و Performance** در jQuery
- **مهاجرت از jQuery به JavaScript مدرن**

---

پروژه‌ها را اجرا کن و اگر خطا یا سؤالی داشتی بفرست. اگر هم خواستی ادامه بدهیم، بگو **«جلسه ۱۰»** (مقایسه با Vanilla JS) یا **«بازبینی پروژه»** تا با هم کدت را بهتر کنیم.



<!-- SOURCE: start.md -->
# File: start.md

<div dir="rtl" style="text-align: right; font-family: 'B Nazanin', Tahoma, sans-serif;">

در ادامه یک دوره آموزشی کامل و ساختاریافته از **jQuery** برای شما تدوین شده است. این دوره از سطح مبتدی شروع شده و تا مباحث پیشرفته و پروژه‌محور ادامه دارد. ساختار آن بر اساس سر فصل‌های استاندارد آموزشی و منابع معتبر jQuery طراحی شده است.

---

## 📚 دوره جامع jQuery: از مبتدی تا پیشرفته

### 🎯 پیش‌نیازهای دوره
- آشنایی مقدماتی با **HTML** و **CSS**
- دانش پایه از **JavaScript** (متغیرها، توابع، شرط‌ها، حلقه‌ها)

---

## فصل ۱: آشنایی با jQuery و راه‌اندازی

### ۱.۱ jQuery چیست و چرا از آن استفاده می‌کنیم؟
- تعریف jQuery به عنوان یک کتابخانه سریع و مختصر جاوااسکریپت
- مزایا: سادگی در نوشتن کد، سازگاری با مرورگرهای مختلف، جامعه بزرگ کاربران، و وجود پلاگین‌های فراوان

### ۱.۲ نصب و افزودن jQuery به صفحه
- دانلود فایل jQuery از سایت رسمی (نسخه فشرده‌شده برای کاهش حجم)
- افزودن از طریق CDN (مثلاً Google CDN)
- قرار دادن تگ `<script>` در HTML و بررسی صحت بارگذاری با کنسول مرورگر (`$` یا `jQuery`)

### ۱.۳ ساختار و سینتکس پایه
- تابع اصلی `$()` و تفاوت آن با `jQuery()`
- رویداد `$(document).ready()` برای اجرای کد پس از آماده شدن DOM
</div> 


```javascript
$(document).ready(function() {
  // کدهای jQuery در اینجا قرار می‌گیرد
});
```
<div dir="rtl" style="text-align: right; font-family: 'B Nazanin', Tahoma, sans-serif;">



---

## فصل ۲: انتخابگرها (Selectors)

### ۲.۱ انتخابگرهای پایه
- انتخاب بر اساس **عنصر** (`$("p")`)، **کلاس** (`$(".myClass")`)، و **شناسه** (`$("#myId")`)
- انتخابگرهای ترکیبی و سلسله‌مراتبی

### ۲.۲ انتخابگرهای پیشرفته
- انتخابگرهای موقعیت (`:first`، `:last`، `:even`، `:odd`)
- انتخابگرهای فرم (`:input`، `:checkbox`، `:selected`)
- انتخابگرهای سفارشی و فیلترها

### ۲.۳ ذخیره‌سازی انتخابگرها (Caching)
- ذخیره نتیجه انتخاب در یک متغیر برای جلوگیری از جستجوی مکرر در DOM

---

## فصل ۳: رویدادها (Events)

### ۳.۱ اتصال رویدادها
- متدهای `click()`، `hover()`، `mouseenter()`، `mouseleave()`
- متد `on()` به عنوان روش مدرن و قدرتمند اتصال رویدادها

### ۳.۲ رویدادهای صفحه‌کلید و فرم
- رویدادهای `keyup`، `keydown`، `keypress`
- رویداد `submit` فرم‌ها و جلوگیری از رفتار پیش‌فرض با `event.preventDefault()`

### ۳.۳ مفاهیم پیشرفته رویداد
- **تفویض رویداد (Event Delegation)** با `on()` برای عناصر پویا
- **فضای نام رویداد (Event Namespace)** برای مدیریت بهتر رویدادها
- **رویدادهای سفارشی** و `trigger()`

---

## فصل ۴: جلوه‌ها و انیمیشن‌ها (Effects & Animations)

### ۴.۱ نمایش و مخفی‌سازی
- `hide()`، `show()`، `toggle()` با کنترل سرعت

### ۴.۲ محو شدن (Fading)
- `fadeIn()`، `fadeOut()`، `fadeToggle()`، `fadeTo()`

### ۴.۳ لغزش (Sliding)
- `slideDown()`، `slideUp()`، `slideToggle()`

### ۴.۴ انیمیشن سفارشی
- متد `animate()` برای ایجاد انیمیشن‌های پیچیده
- مدیریت صف انیمیشن (`queue()`، `dequeue()`، `stop()`، `delay()`)

---

## فصل ۵: دستکاری DOM و محتوا

### ۵.۱ دریافت و تنظیم محتوا
- `text()`، `html()`، `val()` برای خواندن و نوشتن محتوای عناصر

### ۵.۲ افزودن و حذف عناصر
- `append()`، `prepend()`، `after()`، `before()`
- `remove()`، `empty()`، `detach()`

### ۵.۳ کار با کلاس‌ها و ویژگی‌ها (Attributes)

Yes! I’ll be your React instructor. We’ll do this step by step, with small lessons, exercises, and projects. Since you’ve built apps with AI but never learned React, we’ll focus on **understanding what the code is doing**, not just copying it.

## How this course works

- I give you one lesson at a time.
- You type the code yourself, run it, and send me your code or errors.
- I review, correct, and explain.
- We build small projects: profile card → todo app → API app → full app.
- Recommended pace: 30–60 minutes/day for 4–6 weeks.

## Course outline

**Module 0 — JavaScript you need for React**
- let/const, arrow functions, destructuring, spread
- `.map()`, `.filter()`, `.find()`
- import/export
- promises, async/await

**Module 1 — React basics**
- Why React exists
- Components, JSX, props
- Conditional rendering, lists, keys

**Module 2 — State and events**
- `useState`
- Click events, forms, controlled inputs
- Lifting state up

**Module 3 — Effects and data**
- `useEffect`
- Fetching APIs

**Module 4 — Component patterns**

- Context

**Module 5 — Routing and app structure**

- Layouts, pages, protected routes

**Module 6 — Styling and tooling**

**Module 7 — Real project**

**Module 8 — Next steps**

# Lesson 1: React mental model + your first app

## 1. The core idea

React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces.

The main mental model is:

> UI = f(state)

Meaning: your screen is a function of your data. When data changes, React updates the UI.

A React app is made of **components**. A component is a JavaScript function that returns **JSX**.

Example:

```jsx
function Welcome() {
  return <h1>Hello, React!</h1>;
}
```

`Welcome` is a component. It returns JSX that looks like HTML but is actually JavaScript.

## 2. Setup

Install Node.js if you don’t have it. Then in your terminal:

```bash
cd code
npm create vite@latest my-react-app -- --template react
```
```bash
cd my-react-app
npm install
npm run dev
```
---
run to continue develop
```bash
cd code
cd my-react-app
npm run dev
```
Open the local URL it gives you, usually `http://localhost:5173`.

Important files:

- `src/main.jsx` — starts the app
- `src/App.jsx` — your main component
- `src/index.css` — styles

## 3. Your first component edit

Open `src/App.jsx`. Replace everything with:

```jsx
function App() {
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Hello React</h1>
      <p>This is my first component.</p>
    </div>
  );
}

export default App;
```

Save it. The browser should update automatically.

JSX rules to remember:

1. Return **one parent element**.
2. Use `className`, not `class`.
3. Use `{ }` to insert JavaScript.
4. Component names must start with a capital letter.

## 4. Props: passing data into components

Props are like function arguments for components.

```jsx
function Greeting({ name }) {
  return <h1>Hello, {name}!</h1>;
}

function App() {
  return (
    <div>
      <Greeting name="Alex" />
      <Greeting name="Sam" />
      <Greeting name="Taylor" />
    </div>
  );
}

export default App;
```

Here `name` is a prop. Props are **read-only**. A component should never change its own props.

## Your exercise

1. Create a new Vite React app.
2. Replace `App.jsx` with the `Greeting` example above.
3. Create a new component called `UserCard`.
4. `UserCard` should accept these props: `name`, `role`, `age`.
5. Display them like this:

```text
Name: Alex
Role: Developer
Age: 28
```

6. Use `<UserCard />` at least twice with different data.
7. Bonus: if `age >= 18`, show `Adult`; otherwise show `Minor`.

Example structure:

```jsx
function UserCard({ name, role, age }) {
  return (
    <div>
      <h2>{name}</h2>
      <p>Role: {role}</p>
      <p>Age: {age}</p>
    </div>
  );
}
```

Try it yourself before asking me for the answer.

---

When you reply, tell me:

1. Your operating system: Windows, Mac, or Linux?
2. How comfortable are you with JavaScript basics: 1–10?
3. Send me your `App.jsx` code or any error you get.

Then we’ll start Lesson 2: **state and events with `useState`**.

Great! Windows, JS 7/10 — that’s a solid starting point. We can move at a good pace.

## Review of your code

You did a lot right:

- Created two components: `Greeting` and `UserCard`.
- Used props correctly in the function parameters.
- Rendered multiple `Greeting` components.
- Used JSX expressions like `{name}`.

Now let’s fix a few things.

### Issues

1. **Age is passed as a string, not a number.**  
   You wrote `age="35"`. That sends the string `"35"`. For numbers, use curly braces: `age={35}`.

2. **You only used `UserCard` once.**  
   The exercise asked for at least two. That helps you see how reusable components are.

3. **You skipped the bonus.**  
   The bonus was: if `age >= 18`, show `Adult`; otherwise `Minor`. Let’s add that.

4. **No `key` prop needed yet** because we’re not mapping over an array. That’s fine.

### Corrected `App.jsx`

```jsx
function Greeting({ name }) {
  return <h1>Hello, {name}!</h1>;
}

function UserCard({ name, role, age }) {
  return (
    <div>
      <h2>{name}</h2>
      <p>Role: {role}</p>
      <p>Age: {age}</p>
      <p>Status: {age >= 18 ? "Adult" : "Minor"}</p>
    </div>
  );
}

function App() {
  return (
    <div>
      <Greeting name="Alex" />
      <Greeting name="Sam" />
      <Greeting name="Taylor" />

      <UserCard name="Ali" role="manager" age={35} />
      <UserCard name="Sara" role="designer" age={17} />
    </div>
  );
}

export default App;
```

### What to notice

- `age={35}` passes a number.
- `{age >= 18 ? "Adult" : "Minor"}` is a ternary expression inside JSX. It’s a common way to do conditional rendering.
- Props are read-only. You never do `age = 20` inside `UserCard`.

If that makes sense, we move on.

# Lesson 2: State and events with `useState`

## 1. Why state?

So far, our components only display data passed from outside (props).  
But real apps need to **change** over time: a counter, a form, a toggle, a list.

In React, data that can change inside a component is called **state**.

When state changes, React re-renders the component automatically.

## 2. The `useState` hook

We import it from React:

```jsx
import { useState } from "react";
```

Then inside a component:

```jsx
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
```

- `count` is the current value.
- `setCount` is the function you call to update it.
- `0` is the initial value.

**Never** do `count = count + 1`. Always use the setter: `setCount(count + 1)`.

## 3. Example: a simple counter

```jsx
import { useState } from "react";

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>Count: {count}</h2>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>+1</button>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(count - 1)}>-1</button>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(0)}>Reset</button>
    </div>
  );
}

export default Counter;
```

Use it in `App.jsx`:

```jsx
import Counter from "./Counter";

function App() {
  return (
    <div>
      <Counter />
    </div>
  );
}

export default App;
```

### Key points

- `onClick` is a React event prop. It expects a function.
- We use an arrow function: `() => setCount(count + 1)`.  
  If we wrote `onClick={setCount(count + 1)}`, it would run immediately — wrong.
- Each `Counter` component has its own independent state.

## 4. Another example: toggle visibility

```jsx
import { useState } from "react";

function Toggle() {
  const [isVisible, setIsVisible] = useState(true);

  return (
    <div>
      <button onClick={() => setIsVisible(!isVisible)}>
        {isVisible ? "Hide" : "Show"}
      </button>
      {isVisible && <p>Now you see me!</p>}
    </div>
  );
}
```

- `!isVisible` flips true/false.
- `{isVisible && <p>...</p>}` shows the paragraph only when `isVisible` is true.

---

2. Import and use it in `App.jsx`.

4. Create another component `src/Toggle.jsx` with the toggle example.

# Lesson 3: Lists, keys, and rendering multiple items

## 1. The problem

So far you’ve written components by hand:

```jsx
<UserCard name="Ali" role="manager" age={35} />
<UserCard name="Sara" role="designer" age={17} />
```

That works for 2 items. It does **not** work for 50, or for data that comes from an API.  
In React, you almost never write repeated JSX — you **map over an array**.

## 2. `.map()` in JSX

You already know `.map()` from JavaScript. In JSX it returns an array of elements, and React renders each one.

```jsx
const users = [
  { id: 1, name: "Ali", role: "manager", age: 35 },
  { id: 2, name: "Sara", role: "designer", age: 17 },
  { id: 3, name: "Reza", role: "developer", age: 28 },
];

function App() {
  return (
    <div>
      {users.map((user) => (
        <UserCard
          key={user.id}
          name={user.name}
          role={user.role}
          age={user.age}
        />
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}
```

Notice:

- `{ }` lets us run JavaScript inside JSX.
- `.map()` returns an array of `<UserCard />` elements.
- We use **parentheses** after the arrow: `(user) => (` — not `{`. Curly braces would be a function body, not a return.

## 3. Keys — the most common beginner mistake

React needs a **`key`** for each item in a list. It uses keys to know which item is which when the list changes.

Rules:

1. `key` must be **unique among siblings**.
2. `key` must be a **stable** value — usually an `id` from your data.
3. **Do not use the array index** as a key if the list can reorder, filter, or change. Index keys cause subtle bugs (wrong item updating, input values jumping).
4. `key` is not a prop. You can’t read `props.key` inside the component.

Wrong:

```jsx
{users.map((user, index) => <UserCard key={index} ... />)}  // ❌ avoid
```

Right:

```jsx
{users.map((user) => <UserCard key={user.id} ... />)}      // ✅
```

## 4. Filtering and searching

Combining `.filter()` and `.map()` is the bread and butter of React lists.

```jsx
import { useState } from "react";

const users = [
  { id: 1, name: "Ali", role: "manager" },
  { id: 2, name: "Sara", role: "designer" },
  { id: 3, name: "Reza", role: "developer" },
];

function UserList() {
  const [search, setSearch] = useState("");

  const filtered = users.filter((user) =>
    user.name.toLowerCase().includes(search.toLowerCase())
  );

  return (
    <div>
      <input
        value={search}
        onChange={(e) => setSearch(e.target.value)}
        placeholder="Search by name"
      />

      {filtered.length === 0 ? (
        <p>No users found.</p>
      ) : (
        <ul>
          {filtered.map((user) => (
            <li key={user.id}>
              {user.name} — {user.role}
            </li>
          ))}
        </ul>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

export default UserList;
```

Key idea: **don’t modify `users`**. Compute a new array with `.filter()`. React state and props should be treated as read-only.

## 5. Rendering rules to remember

| Situation | How |
|---|---|
| Render array | `{arr.map(item => <X key={item.id} />)}` |
| Show one of two things | `{cond ? <A /> : <B />}` |
| Show or hide | `{cond && <A />}` |
| Empty state | `{arr.length === 0 ? <Empty /> : arr.map(...)}` |
| Nothing to render | return `null` |

Also:

- `false`, `null`, `undefined` render **nothing** in JSX — safe.
- `0` renders as `0` — a classic bug. Use `arr.length > 0 && ...` or a ternary.

## 6. Common pitfalls

1. Forgetting `key` → React warns in the console.
2. Using index as key → bugs when items move.
3. Forgetting `return` inside `.map()` with curly braces:
   ```jsx
   users.map((u) => { <UserCard /> })   // ❌ returns undefined
   users.map((u) => <UserCard />)       // ✅ implicit return
   ```
4. Mutating the array: `users.push(...)`, `users.sort(...)` — don’t. Use `.filter`, `.map`, `.slice`, or a copy.

---

# Lesson 4: Forms and controlled inputs

## 1. The core idea: controlled inputs

In plain HTML, an input keeps its own value. In React, we usually let **state** hold the value:

```jsx
import { useState } from "react";

function NameInput() {
  const [name, setName] = useState("");

  return (
    <input
      value={name}
      onChange={(e) => setName(e.target.value)}
    />
  );
}
```

What happens:

1. You type `a`.
2. `onChange` fires, `e.target.value` is `"a"`.
3. `setName("a")` updates state.
4. Component re-renders.
5. Input's `value` is now `"a"`.

The input **never** holds the truth — React does. That's what "controlled" means.

If you set `value` but forget `onChange`, the input becomes read-only (React warns in the console). If you use `onChange` without `value`, it's an "uncontrolled" input — you lose the ability to read/validate it from state consistently.

**Rule: always pair `value` with `onChange`.**

## 2. Each input type

| Input | Read it via | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| text / email / password / number | `e.target.value` | Always a **string**, even for `type="number"` |
| checkbox | `e.target.checked` | boolean |
| radio | `e.target.value` + `checked` | compare to state |
| select | `e.target.value` | put `value` on the `<select>` |
| textarea | `e.target.value` | in React use `value`, not children |

Examples:

```jsx
// checkbox
const [agreed, setAgreed] = useState(false);
<input
  type="checkbox"
  checked={agreed}
  onChange={(e) => setAgreed(e.target.checked)}
/>
```

```jsx
// select
const [role, setRole] = useState("developer");
<select value={role} onChange={(e) => setRole(e.target.value)}>
  <option value="developer">Developer</option>
  <option value="designer">Designer</option>
  <option value="manager">Manager</option>
</select>
```

```jsx
// radio
const [plan, setPlan] = useState("free");
<label>
  <input
    type="radio"
    name="plan"
    value="free"
    checked={plan === "free"}
    onChange={(e) => setPlan(e.target.value)}
  />
  Free
</label>
<label>
  <input
    type="radio"
    name="plan"
    value="pro"
    checked={plan === "pro"}
    onChange={(e) => setPlan(e.target.value)}
  />
  Pro
</label>
```

```jsx
// textarea
const [bio, setBio] = useState("");
<textarea value={bio} onChange={(e) => setBio(e.target.value)} />
```

## 3. Many fields: one object of state

Once you have 3+ fields, don't create 5 separate `useState` calls. Use **one object**:

```jsx
import { useState } from "react";

const initialForm = {
  name: "",
  email: "",
  age: "",
  role: "developer",
  agreed: false,
};

function RegistrationForm() {
  const [form, setForm] = useState(initialForm);

  function handleChange(e) {
    const { name, value, type, checked } = e.target;
    setForm((prev) => ({
      ...prev,
      [name]: type === "checkbox" ? checked : value,
    }));
  }

  return (
    <form>
      <input name="name"  value={form.name}  onChange={handleChange} placeholder="Name" />
      <input name="email" value={form.email} onChange={handleChange} placeholder="Email" />
      <input name="age"   value={form.age}   onChange={handleChange} placeholder="Age" />

      <select name="role" value={form.role} onChange={handleChange}>
        <option value="developer">Developer</option>
        <option value="designer">Designer</option>
      </select>

      <label>
        <input
          type="checkbox"
          name="agreed"
          checked={form.agreed}
          onChange={handleChange}
        />
        I agree to the terms
      </label>
    </form>
  );
}
```

Things to notice carefully:

**`[name]` is a computed property.** Each input has `name="name"`, `name="email"`, etc. `[name]: value` updates only that key.

**The spread `...prev` is essential.** Without it you'd replace the whole object with just one key. `setForm({ name: value })` would wipe out `email`, `age`, etc.

**The extra parentheses around the returned object.** This:

```jsx
setForm((prev) => ({ ...prev, [name]: value }));
```

…is not the same as:

```jsx
setForm((prev) => { ...prev, [name]: value });  // ❌ syntax error
```

An arrow function with `{` starts a **body**, not an object. You need `({ ... })` to return an object directly. This trips up almost everyone once — when you see a "Unexpected token" error in a setter, check for this.

**Why `(prev) => ...` instead of `setForm({...form, ...})`?** Both usually work, but the functional form is safer when updates happen quickly (e.g. typing fast, or updating in an event handler that fires multiple times). It always sees the latest state. Use it by habit for objects.

## 4. Submitting

```jsx
function handleSubmit(e) {
  e.preventDefault();          // stops the browser from reloading the page
  console.log(form);
}

return <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}> ... </form>;
```

`e.preventDefault()` is **mandatory**. Without it, the browser navigates/reloads and your React state is lost.

A `<button>` inside a `<form>` defaults to `type="submit"`. If you have other buttons inside the form (e.g. "Reset"), give them `type="button"` or they'll also submit.

Reset the form after submit:

```jsx
setForm(initialForm);
```

(Note: `initialForm` is a constant object defined outside the component, so reusing it is safe. Don't reuse a state object directly as your reset value after mutating it — but since we never mutate state, this is fine.)

## 5. Basic validation

Keep it simple for now — validate on submit:

```jsx
function validate(form) {
  const errors = {};
  if (!form.name.trim()) errors.name = "Name is required";
  if (!form.email.includes("@")) errors.email = "Email looks invalid";
  if (!form.age || Number(form.age) < 18) errors.age = "Must be 18 or older";
  if (!form.agreed) errors.agreed = "You must accept the terms";
  return errors;
}
```

```jsx
const [errors, setErrors] = useState({});

function handleSubmit(e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  const nextErrors = validate(form);
  setErrors(nextErrors);
  if (Object.keys(nextErrors).length > 0) return;

  console.log("Submitted:", form);
  setForm(initialForm);
  setErrors({});
}
```

Display them:

```jsx
{errors.name && <p style={{ color: "red" }}>{errors.name}</p>}
```

Remember: `form.age` is a **string**. Always convert with `Number(...)` before comparing numerically. `"20" < 18` is `false`, but `"9" < 18` is also `false` because strings compare alphabetically — a classic bug.

## 6. Common pitfalls (in order of frequency)

1. **Missing `e.preventDefault()`** → page reloads, state lost.
2. **Missing parens around returned object in `setForm`** → syntax error.
3. **Missing `...prev`** → only one field survives.
4. **Missing `onChange`** → input is frozen.
5. **Treating `age` as a number** → `form.age < 18` compares strings.
6. **Missing `name` attribute on inputs** → the `[name]: value` trick breaks.
7. **Mutating state directly** — `form.name = "x"` does nothing; React won't re-render. Always go through `setForm`.

---

|---|---|---|
| name | text | required |

| age | number | required, must be ≥ 18 |

| bio | textarea | optional |

# Lesson 5: `useEffect` — side effects and fetching data

Before we start: you now have Lessons 1–4 of material and no exercise code sent back. That's okay — but this lesson is **harder** than the previous ones and it's very easy to *think* you understand `useEffect` without actually being able to use it. `useEffect` is the #1 source of bugs for React beginners: infinite loops, stale data, memory leaks. Please build the exercise after reading this. Even a broken attempt teaches you more than five clean readings.

Now, the lesson.

---

## 1. What is a "side effect"?

A **side effect** is anything a component does that isn't "compute JSX from props/state." Examples:

- Fetching data from a server
- Setting a `setTimeout` / `setInterval`
- Reading/writing `localStorage`
- Adding an event listener on `window`
- Changing `document.title`
- Subscribing to a websocket

Rendering must be **pure**: same props + state → same JSX, no side effects. Side effects go in `useEffect`.

> Rule of thumb: if you're about to do something that reaches *outside* React, it goes in `useEffect`.

## 2. The shape of `useEffect`

```jsx
import { useEffect } from "react";

useEffect(() => {
  // side effect goes here
  return () => {
    // optional cleanup: runs before the next effect and on unmount
  };
}, [dependencies]);
```

Two things are always true:

1. **The effect runs after render.** Not during. React first renders the JSX to the screen, *then* runs the effect.
2. **The dependency array controls when it runs.**

### Dependency array rules (memorize these)

| Array | When the effect runs |
|---|---|
| `[]` (empty) | Once, after the first render only |
| `[a, b]` | After first render, and again whenever `a` or `b` **changes** |
| *(omitted)* | After **every** render — almost always a bug |

"Changes" means: compared with the previous render using `Object.is`. Primitives compare by value, objects/arrays/functions by reference.

## 3. The four classic patterns

### Pattern 1: run once on mount

```jsx
useEffect(() => {
  console.log("Mounted");
}, []);
```

### Pattern 2: react to a value changing

```jsx
const [query, setQuery] = useState("");

useEffect(() => {
  console.log("Query changed:", query);
}, [query]);
```

### Pattern 3: cleanup (intervals, timers, listeners)

```jsx
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => {
    console.log("tick");
  }, 1000);

  return () => clearInterval(id);
}, []);
```

Without `clearInterval`, the interval keeps running after the component disappears → memory leak. This is what the cleanup function is for. **Any effect that "starts something" must return a function that "stops it."**

### Pattern 4: fetch data

```jsx
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

function UserList() {
  const [users, setUsers] = useState([]);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    let cancelled = false;

    async function load() {
      try {
        setLoading(true);
        setError(null);
        const res = await fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users");
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
        const data = await res.json();
        if (!cancelled) setUsers(data);
      } catch (err) {
        if (!cancelled) setError(err.message);
      } finally {
        if (!cancelled) setLoading(false);
      }
    }

    load();

    return () => {
      cancelled = true;
    };
  }, []);

  if (loading) return <p>Loading…</p>;
  if (error) return <p style={{ color: "red" }}>Error: {error}</p>;

  return (
    <ul>
      {users.map((u) => (
        <li key={u.id}>{u.name}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
```

**Why `let cancelled`?** If the user navigates away (or the deps change) while the fetch is in-flight, the cleanup runs and sets `cancelled = true`. The fetch still resolves, but we skip `setState` — avoiding a "state update on an unmounted component" warning and stale data overwriting fresh data.

**Why can't the effect callback be `async`?** Because it must return either nothing or a cleanup function — an `async` function returns a **promise**. So we define an inner async function `load()` and call it.

**Why the three states (`users`, `loading`, `error`)?** Because a fetch has three phases: *loading*, *success*, *failure*. Always model all three. A fetch that only sets `data` on success will show an empty list forever if the request fails.

## 4. The infinite loop — the #1 `useEffect` bug

```jsx
useEffect(() => {
  setUsers([...users, newUser]);  // ❌
}, [users]);                       // deps: users
```

`users` changes → effect runs → sets `users` → `users` changed → effect runs → …**infinite loop**.

Two fixes depending on intent:

- **You don't want it to react to `users`:** remove `users` from deps (usually correct).
- **You genuinely want to append once:** move the append into an event handler (e.g. `handleAddUser`), *not* an effect. Effects are for **synchronizing with the outside world**, not for deriving state from state.

> **Big principle:** if you're computing one piece of state from another, you usually **don't need `useEffect` at all** — just compute it during render:
>
> ```jsx
> const [users, setUsers] = useState(allUsers);
> const filtered = users.filter(u => u.name.includes(search));  // no effect needed
> ```
>
> Lesson 3's exercise already did this. That's the right pattern. Only reach for `useEffect` when you actually need to *interact with the outside world*.

## 5. Other classic pitfalls

1. **Missing deps** → stale values.
   ```jsx
   useEffect(() => {
     document.title = `You typed: ${query}`;  // query is used
   }, []);                                     // ❌ query missing
   ```
   ESLint will flag this. Trust the linter.

2. **Object/array/function in deps** → runs every render, because they're new references each time.
   ```jsx
   useEffect(() => { ... }, [{}]);          // ❌ new object each render
   useEffect(() => { ... }, [fetchData]);   // ❌ if fetchData is defined inside the component, new each render
   ```
   Fix: move the function inside the effect, or wrap with `useCallback` (later lesson).

3. **Setting state unconditionally in a fetch effect with a dependency on that state** → loop again. Same rule as §4.

4. **Forgetting cleanup for `setInterval` / `addEventListener`** → leak. Symmetry rule: every `+` in the effect needs a `-` in the cleanup.

5. **StrictMode double-invoke.** In dev, React 18 runs effects **twice** (mount → unmount → mount) to surface bugs. Your effect must be idempotent, and your cleanup must be real. If you see double console logs in dev — that's expected, not a bug.

## 6. When you should NOT use `useEffect`

Because beginners overuse it, here's the list:

- **Deriving values from props/state** → just compute during render.
- **Resetting state when a prop changes** → use `key` on the component, or compute directly.
- **Handling user events** → put it in the event handler (`onClick`, `onSubmit`).
- **"Run once after mount" for setting up a variable** → not a side effect; just initialize with `useState(initialValue)`.

Use `useEffect` only for *synchronizing with something outside React*: network, DOM APIs, browser APIs, timers, third-party libraries.

# Lesson 6: Putting it all together — a real CRUD app

**Quick honest check-in.** You're now six lessons in with no code sent back. I'll keep teaching — that's not a threat — but Lesson 6 is the one where the previous five *have* to be in your hands. It combines props (L1), state (L2), lists + keys (L3), forms (L4), and effects/fetch (L5). Reading it will feel great. Building it will feel harder. Building it is the point.

Here's what I suggest: after you read this, spend one hour building **one** thing — the add-task handler — even if the rest of the app is broken. Send me that. We'll grow from there. That one hour is worth more than the next two lessons.

Now, the lesson.

---

## 1. What we're building

A **tasks app**:

- Fetches 5 seed tasks from a public API on mount
- Lets you **add** a task via a form
- Lets you **toggle** done/not-done
- Lets you **delete** a task
- Filter bar: `All` / `Active` / `Done`, with counts

It sounds small. It is small. But it touches **every concept** we've covered, and every bug you'll hit is a bug you'll hit in real code forever.

Why this matters: you've been using AI to generate apps. After this lesson you can *read* that generated code — spot a mutated array, a missing `key`, a `useEffect` that shouldn't exist.

## 2. The architecture question: where does state live?

> **Rule:** state lives in the **lowest common ancestor** of all components that need it.

Who needs the task list?

- `App` (renders the list and the counts)
- `TaskItem` (each row needs its task + a way to delete/toggle it)
- `TaskForm` (needs to add to the list)

The common ancestor is `App`. So `App` owns `tasks`. Children receive data and functions as **props**.

```
App  ←── owns state
├── TaskForm     (prop: onAdd)
├── FilterBar    (props: filter, onChange, counts)
└── TaskItem[]   (props: task, onToggle, onDelete)
```

This is the pattern called **"data down, actions up."** State flows down as props. Events flow up as callbacks.

Children **never** mutate the parent's state directly. They call the function the parent gave them. That function is defined in `App`, so it has access to `setTasks`.

```jsx
// in App
function handleDelete(id) { setTasks(prev => prev.filter(t => t.id !== id)); }

// passed down
<TaskItem task={t} onDelete={handleDelete} />

// in TaskItem
<button onClick={() => onDelete(task.id)}>Delete</button>
```

## 3. The immutable-update cheat sheet (memorize this)

Almost every bug in a task app is a mutation bug. Print this:

| Goal | Code |
|---|---|
| **Add** an item | `prev => [...prev, newItem]` |
| **Delete** an item | `prev => prev.filter(x => x.id !== id)` |
| **Update** one item | `prev => prev.map(x => x.id === id ? { ...x, done: !x.done } : x)` |
| **Sort** | `prev => [...prev].sort((a, b) => ...)` |
| **Reverse** | `prev => [...prev].reverse()` |

Notice the two verbs that **never** appear: `push` and `splice`. They mutate. React will not re-render if you mutate the existing array — the reference hasn't changed.

And for **nested** objects (like updating just `done`), you must spread:

```jsx
{ ...task, done: !task.done }  // ✅ a new task object with flipped done
{ done: !task.done }           // ❌ loses title and id
task.done = !task.done         // ❌ mutation, no re-render
```

Also: inside the updater, always use `prev =>`, not `tasks` directly — `prev` is guaranteed to be the *latest* value, `tasks` might be stale in a rapid sequence of updates.

## 4. What happens after the fetch?

You fetch 5 tasks. Then the user adds a new one. Two schools of thought:

**Refetch after every change.** Send the change to the server, then re-run `GET /tasks`. Correct for a real API. Slow. More code.

**Update local state only.** Fetch once, then `setTasks` for all changes. Fast. Simple. **This is what we'll do for this exercise** — because the exercise is about state management, not API writing.

Real apps use a hybrid: `POST` to server, then update local state from the response (or optimistically, then reconcile). We cover that when you're ready for React Query. For now, local state after fetch is the right call.

One consequence to notice: if you refresh the page, your added tasks disappear. That's *correct behavior* for this exercise — we're not persisting yet. `localStorage` is a fun bonus (see §7).

## 5. The skeleton (with two handlers left for you)

Files:

```
src/
  App.jsx
  TaskForm.jsx
  TaskItem.jsx
```

### `App.jsx`

```jsx
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";
import TaskForm from "./TaskForm";
import TaskItem from "./TaskItem";

function App() {
  const [tasks, setTasks] = useState([]);
  const [filter, setFilter] = useState("all");   // "all" | "active" | "done"
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    let cancelled = false;
    async function load() {
      try {
        setLoading(true);
        const res = await fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos?_limit=5");
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
        const data = await res.json();
        if (!cancelled) {
          setTasks(data.map(t => ({ id: t.id, title: t.title, done: t.completed })));
        }
      } catch (err) {
        if (!cancelled) setError(err.message);
      } finally {
        if (!cancelled) setLoading(false);
      }
    }
    load();
    return () => { cancelled = true; };
  }, []);

  // ---- handlers ----
  function handleAdd(title) {
    // YOUR CODE — hint: setTasks(prev => [...prev, { id: crypto.randomUUID(), title, done: false }])
  }

  function handleToggle(id) {
    // YOUR CODE — hint: setTasks(prev => prev.map(t => t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t))
  }

  function handleDelete(id) {
    setTasks(prev => prev.filter(t => t.id !== id));   // worked example
  }

  // ---- derived values (NOT in useEffect!) ----
  const visible = tasks.filter(t =>
    filter === "all"    ? true :
    filter === "active" ? !t.done :
    /* done */            t.done
  );
  const counts = {
    all: tasks.length,
    active: tasks.filter(t => !t.done).length,
    done: tasks.filter(t => t.done).length,
  };

  if (loading) return <p>Loading…</p>;
  if (error) return <p style={{ color: "red" }}>Error: {error}</p>;

  return (
    <div style={{ maxWidth: 480, margin: "40px auto" }}>
      <h1>Tasks</h1>
      <TaskForm onAdd={handleAdd} />

      <div>
        {["all", "active", "done"].map(f => (
          <button
            key={f}
            onClick={() => setFilter(f)}
            style={{ fontWeight: filter === f ? "bold" : "normal" }}
          >
            {f} ({counts[f]})
          </button>
        ))}
      </div>

      {visible.length === 0 ? (
        <p>No tasks here.</p>
      ) : (
        <ul>
          {visible.map(t => (
            <TaskItem
              key={t.id}
              task={t}
              onToggle={handleToggle}
              onDelete={handleDelete}
            />
          ))}
        </ul>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

export default App;
```

### `TaskForm.jsx`

```jsx
import { useState } from "react";

function TaskForm({ onAdd }) {
  const [title, setTitle] = useState("");

  function handleSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    const trimmed = title.trim();
    if (!trimmed) return;
    onAdd(trimmed);
    setTitle("");
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <input
        value={title}
        onChange={(e) => setTitle(e.target.value)}
        placeholder="What needs doing?"
      />
      <button type="submit">Add</button>
    </form>
  );
}

export default TaskForm;
```

Note: `TaskForm` does **not** own the task list. It owns only its own input text. When submitted, it calls `onAdd(title)` — the parent handles the rest. That's the pattern.

### `TaskItem.jsx`

```jsx
function TaskItem({ task, onToggle, onDelete }) {
  return (
    <li>
      <input
        type="checkbox"
        checked={task.done}
        onChange={() => onToggle(task.id)}
      />
      <span style={{ textDecoration: task.done ? "line-through" : "none" }}>
        {task.title}
      </span>
      <button onClick={() => onDelete(task.id)}>✕</button>
    </li>
  );
}

export default TaskItem;
```

Note the two `onClick`/`onChange` handlers pass `task.id` — the parent doesn't need to know which task it is, the child knows.

## 6. Common pitfalls (you will hit at least three)

1. **`prev.map` returns the item, not the JSX.** If your toggle button suddenly renders `[object Object]` you've got a JSX/object mix-up.
2. **Missing `...t` in the toggle updater** — every other field vanishes from that row.
3. **`handleAdd` called with the whole event instead of the string** — because you wrote `onSubmit={onAdd}` somewhere by mistake. Pass the value, not the event.
4. **Filter counts frozen** — because you put them in `useState` and never updated them, or in a `useEffect`. Just compute them during render. The comment says so.
5. **Filter buttons with no visible change** — because `setFilter(f)` was written as `setFilter(f())` (calling f) or `setFilter` alone (returning the setter).
6. **`key` on the `<ul>`** instead of the `<TaskItem>` — the key belongs on the outermost element *inside* `.map()`.
7. **Refreshing the page and the list is empty** — you commented out the fetch by accident. It happens.

## 7. Extras (only after the base app works)

Do these in order. They are small on purpose. Each one tests a different lesson.

- **A.** Persist to `localStorage`. `useEffect(() => localStorage.setItem("tasks", JSON.stringify(tasks)), [tasks])` for saving; read from `localStorage` in the initial state of `useState`. Bonus question: **does `localStorage.getItem` count as a side effect?** (Hint: technically yes, but it's synchronous and it's an initializer — the `useState(() => ...)` lazy initializer form is acceptable.)
- **B.** Edit task titles in place. Click the title → becomes an `<input>` → Enter saves, Escape cancels. This uses a **local editing state inside `TaskItem`** — no lifting needed.
- **C.** Clear all completed. One button. `setTasks(prev => prev.filter(t => !t.done))`. One line.
- **D.** Add a `"Clear all"` and confirm it works with the filter still set to `"done"` — does the empty state message appear correctly?

---

## Your exercise

1. Build the app above, filling in `handleAdd` and `handleToggle`.
2. Verify all four operations work: fetch, add, toggle, delete.
3. Verify the filter bar and counts.
4. Do **A** (localStorage) if you finish early.
5. Then send me:
    - `App.jsx`, `TaskForm.jsx`, `TaskItem.jsx`
    - One-sentence answer to **"Why does `handleAdd` use `prev =>` instead of just `tasks =>`?"**
    - Any console warnings or errors, pasted exactly.

If your app doesn't work yet, send it anyway with a note about what *should* happen vs what *does*. That's a real question and a real answer.

**Next: Lesson 7 — React Router.** Multi-page apps, nested routes, URL params, and why `<a href>` is a bug in a React app. After that, you'll have built something real, and Lesson 8 will be your first project **without me writing the code.**

# File: 7.md

# Lesson 7: React Router — multi-page apps

*(Short note, then we teach: seven lessons, zero code back. I'll keep offering these — but at some point the course becomes a book you're reading rather than a skill you're building. This lesson is genuinely useful only if you type it. One route, one `<Link>`, one `useParams` — that's a valid start.)*

---

## 1. Why not `<a href>`?

In a normal website, `<a href="/tasks">` makes the browser request a new HTML page from the server. In a React app, you have **one HTML page**. There is no `/tasks` file on the server. If you click that `<a>`, you get a 404, or the dev server serves the same page but **all your React state is wiped**.

React Router solves this:

- It intercepts clicks on special links (`<Link>`).
- It changes the URL using the browser's History API — **no page reload**.
- It reads the URL and decides which component to render.

The URL becomes **part of your app's state.** That's the mental model: routing is state management for the address bar.

## 2. Install

```bash
npm install react-router-dom
```

## 3. The simplest possible router

`src/main.jsx`:

```jsx
import React from "react";
import ReactDOM from "react-dom/client";
import { BrowserRouter } from "react-router-dom";
import App from "./App";
import "./index.css";

ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById("root")).render(
  <React.StrictMode>
    <BrowserRouter>
      <App />
    </BrowserRouter>
  </React.StrictMode>
);
```

`BrowserRouter` must wrap everything that uses routing. **Common bug #1:** forgetting this, then getting `useRoutes() may be used only in the context of a <Router> component`.

`src/App.jsx`:

```jsx
import { Routes, Route, Link } from "react-router-dom";
import Home from "./pages/Home";
import Tasks from "./pages/Tasks";
import About from "./pages/About";

function App() {
  return (
    <div>
      <nav>
        <Link to="/">Home</Link>
        <Link to="/tasks">Tasks</Link>
        <Link to="/about">About</Link>
      </nav>

      <Routes>
        <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
        <Route path="/tasks" element={<Tasks />} />
        <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
        <Route path="*" element={<p>Page not found (404)</p>} />
      </Routes>
    </div>
  );
}

export default App;
```

That's the whole core. `<Routes>` is a switch — it picks **one** matching `<Route>`. `<Route path="*" element={...}>` is the 404 fallback; always include it.

`<Link to="/tasks">` is the router's `<a>`. Always use it inside a React app. If you must use `<a>` (e.g. external URL), that's fine — but for internal navigation, `<Link>`.

## 4. `NavLink` — links that know they're active

`<NavLink>` adds an `active` class automatically.

```jsx
import { NavLink } from "react-router-dom";

<NavLink to="/tasks" className={({ isActive }) => isActive ? "active" : ""}>
  Tasks
</NavLink>
```

You'll use this for every nav menu you ever build. Style `.active` in CSS and you're done.

## 5. URL parameters — `useParams`

Routes can have **dynamic segments**:

```jsx
<Route path="/tasks/:id" element={<TaskDetails />} />
```

Now in `TaskDetails`:

```jsx
import { useParams } from "react-router-dom";

function TaskDetails() {
  const { id } = useParams();   // string! "5", not 5
  // fetch the task by id, or find it in a shared store
  return <h1>Task {id}</h1>;
}
```

Two things to internalize:

1. **`id` is a string.** Comparing `task.id === id` will be `false` if `task.id` is a number. Convert: `Number(id)`.
2. **If the URL changes (e.g. `/tasks/1` → `/tasks/2`), React reuses the same component.** If you fetch by id, put `id` in the effect's deps — otherwise you'll show the first task forever. This is the *one* time the effect deps rule genuinely matters:

```jsx
useEffect(() => {
  // fetch task by id
}, [id]);   // ← required
```

## 6. `useNavigate` — navigate from code

Sometimes you want to navigate after an action (e.g. after submitting a form):

```jsx
import { useNavigate } from "react-router-dom";

function NewTask() {
  const navigate = useNavigate();

  function handleSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    // ... save it
    navigate("/tasks");   // or navigate(`/tasks/${newId}`)
  }
}
```

`navigate(-1)` goes back. `navigate("/tasks", { replace: true })` replaces the history entry instead of adding one — good for redirects after login.

## 7. Nested routes and layouts — `Outlet`

This is the feature that makes router code *clean*. Instead of repeating `<nav>` on every page:

```jsx
// App.jsx
import { Routes, Route, Outlet, Link } from "react-router-dom";

function Layout() {
  return (
    <div>
      <nav>
        <Link to="/">Home</Link>
        <Link to="/tasks">Tasks</Link>
        <Link to="/tasks/new">New</Link>
      </nav>
      <Outlet />   {/* ← child routes render here */}
    </div>
  );
}

export default function App() {
  return (
    <Routes>
      <Route element={<Layout />}>
        <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
        <Route path="/tasks" element={<Tasks />} />
        <Route path="/tasks/new" element={<NewTask />} />
        <Route path="/tasks/:id" element={<TaskDetails />} />
        <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
      </Route>
    </Routes>
  );
}
```

The `<Route element={<Layout />}>` wrapper has **no `path`** — it's a *layout route*. Every child renders inside its `<Outlet />`. Change the nav once, it's everywhere.

## 8. Where does the URL go? Query strings — `useSearchParams`

For **filters**, query strings are better than params — they're shareable and optional:

```jsx
import { useSearchParams } from "react-router-dom";

function Tasks() {
  const [searchParams, setSearchParams] = useSearchParams();
  const filter = searchParams.get("filter") ?? "all";   // "all" | "active" | "done"

  function setFilter(next) {
    setSearchParams({ filter: next });
  }

  // ...use `filter` instead of useState
}
```

Notice the pattern: **the URL replaces `useState`** for the filter. Refresh the page → the filter is still there. Send the link to a friend → same view. That's why routing is state management.

**This is a direct upgrade to Lesson 6's tasks app.** Same UI, `filter` moves from `useState` to the URL. That's the exercise below.

## 9. Common pitfalls (all of them are real)

1. **Missing `<BrowserRouter>`** — everything breaks with a hook-context error.
2. **`<a href>` instead of `<Link>`** — page reload, state gone.
3. **`useParams` returns strings** — always cast.
4. **Forgetting `[id]` in the deps of a fetch-by-id effect** — shows stale task.
5. **No `path="*"` route** — navigating to a bad URL shows a blank page.
6. **Wrapping `<Routes>` in a component outside the `<BrowserRouter>`** in the tree — hooks lose context.
7. **Order of routes with overlapping paths** — React Router 6+ picks the most specific match, so you usually *don't* need to worry, but `/tasks/new` and `/tasks/:id` both matching `/tasks/new` is a classic — React Router prefers the static one, but if you're ever confused, check specificity.
8. **Using `window.location.href`** for navigation — reloads the app. Use `navigate()`.
9. **`<Route>` children must be `element={<X />}`** — not `component={X}` (that's the v5 API, still copied around a lot; if a tutorial says `component=`, it's out of date).

## 10. Your exercise

Take the **Lesson 6 tasks app** and add routing:

1. Install `react-router-dom`. Wrap in `<BrowserRouter>` in `main.jsx`.
2. Create a `<Layout>` with `<NavLink>` for Home / Tasks / About.
3. Routes:
    - `/` → Home (a few sentences)
    - `/tasks` → the tasks list
    - `/tasks/:id` → a **task detail page**. If the user is on the list and clicks a task's title, navigate there. Show title + done status.
    - `*` → 404 page
4. **Upgrade the filter** to `useSearchParams` as in §8. Verify:
    - clicking a filter button updates the URL (e.g. `?filter=active`)
    - refreshing the page keeps the filter
    - the counts still work
5. **Bonus:** On `/tasks/:id`, add a "← Back to tasks" button that calls `navigate(-1)`.

### What I'll check when you send it

- Is `BrowserRouter` above the tree that uses `<Routes>`?
- Is every internal link a `<Link>`/`<NavLink>` — no `<a href="/tasks">` anywhere?
- Does `/tasks/:id` correctly cast `id` to a number before comparing with `task.id`?
- Does the filter survive a page refresh (i.e. is it really in the URL)?
- Is there a `*` route?

Send me:
- `main.jsx`, `App.jsx`, `pages/*.jsx` (or a link — a GitHub repo is fine)
- A screenshot or paste of the URL after clicking the filter buttons.

**Next: Lesson 8 — your first project, written by you, not by me.** You pick the app (from a short list I'll give you), you write the code, you send it, I review it like a senior dev would. No new concepts — just everything you've learned, applied. That's the lesson that makes this course stick.



<!-- SOURCE: 8.md -->
# File: 8.md

# Lesson 8: Your first project — written by you

No new concepts today. Everything you need you already have: components, props, `useState`, lists and keys, forms, `useEffect`, and routing. Today you **combine** them into something that's yours.

This lesson is different in shape. There's no code to copy. There's a spec, a build order, and a review rubric. Your job is to build. Mine is to review what you send.

I've said this a few times already, so I'll say it once and then drop it: **you can't learn to build React apps by reading about building React apps.** If you take nothing else from this course, take this: the gap between "I understand the lesson" and "I can build the thing" is where all the learning is. You close it by writing code that breaks, reading the error, and fixing it.

---

## 1. Pick one project

### Option A — Book Library *(recommended)*

A personal reading tracker.

- Add a book: title, author, status (`want` / `reading` / `finished`), rating (1–5, only when finished)
- List all books as cards
- Filter by status tabs with counts
- Search by title or author
- Click a book → detail page at `/books/:id`
- Delete from the list or the detail page
- Persist to `localStorage`

**Why this one:** it has every skill except fetch, and every update you'll make is a nested-object update — the thing that breaks most beginners. Rating only applies to finished books, so you'll deal with conditional UI.

### Option B — Quiz App

10 hardcoded questions, one at a time, multiple choice. Score at the end, restart button. **Different shape:** no lists, no CRUD — it's a state machine (`questionIndex`, `answers`, `finished`). Good if you're tired of list apps. Harder to make impressive, easier to make correct.

### Option C — Weather Dashboard

Search a city, fetch current weather + 5-day forecast from a free API (Open-Meteo needs no key). Save favourite cities to `localStorage`. Recent searches as chips. **Mostly about async:** loading/error/empty states, debouncing the search, refetching when the city changes.

Pick **A** unless you have a reason not to. The rest of this lesson is written for A.

---

## 2. The spec (Option A)

### Data model

```js
{
  id: "uuid-string",
  title: "The Pragmatic Programmer",
  author: "Hunt & Thomas",
  status: "want" | "reading" | "finished",
  rating: 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5,   // 0 = not rated
  createdAt: 1699999999999         // ms timestamp, for sorting
}
```

Decide this **first** and write it down in a comment at the top of `App.jsx`. Half of all bugs come from a data model that wasn't decided up front.

### Routes

| Path | Page | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `/` | Home / redirect to `/books` | A one-line welcome is fine |
| `/books` | Library list | Filter + search live here |
| `/books/:id` | Book detail | Show all fields; delete; change status |
| `*` | 404 | |

Filter and search go in the URL (`?status=reading&q=pragmatic`), not `useState` — Lesson 7, §8.

### Rules

- Status and rating: `rating` only settable when `status === "finished"`. Changing status away from `finished` resets rating to `0`. *(This is a real product decision, not just an exercise — it forces you to think about derived vs. stored state.)*
- Filter tabs always show counts: `All (8) · Want (3) · Reading (2) · Finished (3)`.
- Search matches title **or** author, case-insensitive.
- Empty states: no books at all, and no results for the current filter/search. Two different messages.
- Persist to `localStorage` on every change; hydrate from it on mount. Use the **lazy initializer** form: `useState(() => loadFromStorage())` — not a `useEffect` that sets state on mount. *(If you don't remember why, re-read Lesson 6 §7.)*

### Files

```
src/
  main.jsx
  App.jsx
  pages/
    Home.jsx
    BookList.jsx
    BookDetail.jsx
    NotFound.jsx
  components/
    Layout.jsx
    BookCard.jsx
    BookForm.jsx
    FilterBar.jsx
  lib/
    storage.js      // load/save helpers
    books.js        // pure helpers: filterBooks, counts, etc. (optional but good)
```

---

## 3. Build order (this is the important part)

Beginners try to build everything at once and drown. Do it in this order. **Get each step working before starting the next.** Commit to git after each step if you're using git.

1. **Shell.** Vite app, router, `Layout`, four empty pages, nav links. Click around, confirm no console errors, 404 works.
2. **Data model + fake data.** In `App.jsx`, `useState` with 3 hardcoded books. No form, no storage yet.
3. **List.** `BookList` renders `BookCard` for each book. Hardcode nothing in `BookCard` — all via props. Check the `key` warning is gone.
4. **Filter tabs.** Status in the URL. Counts computed from `books` during render. No search yet.
5. **Search.** Query in the URL. Both filters combine. Empty state message.
6. **Add form.** On `/books`, a form above the list. Adds to state. Doesn't persist yet — refresh loses it, and that's fine for now.
7. **Delete.** Button on each card.
8. **Status change.** On the card or the detail page — your choice. Remember the rating rule.
9. **Detail page.** `/books/:id`, `useParams`, cast the id, find the book, render fields. Handle "id not found" (someone typed a bad URL).
10. **Persistence.** `localStorage` save on change, lazy-init load on mount.
11. **Polish.** Empty states, disabled submit when title is blank, loading nothing (no fetch here), keyboard-friendly. Optional: sort by `createdAt` desc.

Notice the order: **UI → data → interaction → persistence.** Beginners usually start with persistence and the form. Don't.

---

## 4. Self-review before you send it

Answer each of these honestly. If any answer is "no" or "I'm not sure", fix it before sending.

**State**
- [ ] Is `books` state in exactly one place (`App`)?
- [ ] Are `visibleBooks` and `counts` **computed during render**, not stored in state and not in a `useEffect`?
- [ ] Is there any `useEffect` at all? *(Correct answer for this project: probably zero or one, for `localStorage`. If you have three, you're deriving state — Lesson 5 §6.)*
- [ ] Do all updates use `prev => ...` and spread (`[...prev, x]`, `{ ...book, status }`)?
- [ ] Zero occurrences of `.push(`, `.splice(`, or `book.status = ` anywhere?

**Lists**
- [ ] Is `key` on the element returned by `.map()`, using `book.id`?
- [ ] Zero uses of the array index as `key`?

**Forms**
- [ ] `e.preventDefault()` in `onSubmit`?
- [ ] Inputs are controlled — `value` + `onChange` on every one?
- [ ] Rating is only editable when status is `finished`?

**Routing**
- [ ] `<BrowserRouter>` in `main.jsx` above everything?
- [ ] All internal navigation via `<Link>` / `<NavLink>` / `navigate()`, no `<a href>`?
- [ ] `id` from `useParams` cast with `Number()` (or compared as string consistently)?
- [ ] Filter and search in the URL — refresh keeps them?
- [ ] `*` route exists?

**Hygiene**
- [ ] Console is clean — no key warnings, no "setState on unmounted", no controlled/uncontrolled input warnings?
- [ ] No commented-out dead code left behind?
- [ ] Component names capitalized, files named consistently?

---

## 5. What to send me

Send all of:

1. **The code** — paste the files, or a GitHub repo link, or a CodeSandbox/StackBlitz link. Any of those is fine.
2. **The URL state** — what the address bar shows after: (a) clicking "Reading", (b) typing `tol` in search, (c) both.
3. **Console output** — paste it exactly, including warnings in yellow. Don't clean it up.
4. **A three-line honest report:**
    - What works.
    - What doesn't work (be specific: "clicking delete on the detail page deletes, but the page doesn't go anywhere" is useful; "it's broken" isn't).
    - What you're least sure about.

I'll review it the way I'd review a colleague's PR: things that are wrong, things that are risky, things that are good, and the one thing to fix first. Then we go to **Lesson 9 — testing and refactoring your own project** (yes, we refactor *your* code, not mine).

---

### If you're stuck before starting

That's normal and it's not a reason to skip. Do this instead: send me **your Lesson 6 tasks app**, working or not, with the four-line report above. We'll debug it together, and *that* conversation will unblock the project. Building a small broken thing with feedback beats building a big perfect thing alone.

You've got this. Start with step 1 — router + four empty pages. Send me that if you want a quick check-in before going further.

# Changelog

> **Tags:**
> - :boom:       [Breaking Change]
> - :eyeglasses: [Spec Compliance]
> - :rocket:     [New Feature]
> - :bug:        [Bug Fix]
> - :memo:       [Documentation]
> - :house:      [Internal]
> - :nail_care:  [Polish]

> Semver Policy: https://github.com/babel/babel/tree/main/packages/babel-parser#semver

_Note: Gaps between patch versions are faulty, broken or test releases._

See the [Babel Changelog](https://github.com/babel/babel/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) for the pre-6.8.0 version Changelog.

## 6.17.1 (2017-05-10)

### :bug: Bug Fix
 * Fix typo in flow spread operator error (Brian Ng)
 * Fixed invalid number literal parsing ([#473](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/473)) (Alex Kuzmenko)
 * Fix number parser ([#433](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/433)) (Alex Kuzmenko)
 * Ensure non pattern shorthand props are checked for reserved words ([#479](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/479)) (Brian Ng)
 * Remove jsx context when parsing arrow functions ([#475](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/475)) (Brian Ng)
 * Allow super in class properties ([#499](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/499)) (Brian Ng)
 * Allow flow class field to be named constructor ([#510](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/510)) (Brian Ng)

## 6.17.0 (2017-04-20)

### :bug: Bug Fix
 * Cherry-pick #418 to 6.x ([#476](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/476)) (Sebastian McKenzie)
 * Add support for invalid escapes in tagged templates ([#274](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/274)) (Kevin Gibbons)
 * Throw error if new.target is used outside of a function ([#402](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/402)) (Brian Ng)
 * Fix parsing of class properties ([#351](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/351)) (Kevin Gibbons)
 * Fix parsing yield with dynamicImport ([#383](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/383)) (Brian Ng)
 * Ensure consistent start args for parseParenItem ([#386](https://github.com/babel/babylon/pull/386)) (Brian Ng)

## 7.0.0-beta.8 (2017-04-04)
